#5729. A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength

A simple daily fiber supplement may offer a surprising new way to relieve knee arthritis pain while improving muscle strength. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Nottingham, people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) who took a prebiotic fiber called inulin experienced significant reductions in pain, improved grip strength, and decreased sensitivity to pain.

The supplement also appeared to be considerably easier for participants to stick with than a digital physical therapy program. Only 3.6% of those assigned to inulin alone dropped out of the study, compared with 21% of those assigned to physical therapy alone.

Published in the journal Nutrients, the findings suggest that improving gut health could become an additional strategy for managing arthritis. They also reveal an intriguing connection between the bacteria living in our digestive system, the way our bodies process pain, and muscle function.

A Simple Dietary Change Could Help Relieve Arthritis Pain

Knee osteoarthritis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and is a major cause of chronic pain and disability, especially among older adults. The condition develops as the tissues within the knee joint, including the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorate. This can lead to pain, stiffness, swelling, and difficulty with everyday activities such as walking or climbing stairs.

Treatment typically focuses on reducing symptoms and maintaining mobility. Pain medications can provide relief but may cause unwanted side effects, while physical therapy and regular exercise can help improve joint function. However, keeping up with an exercise program can be difficult, particularly for people already struggling with persistent pain.

The new research raises the possibility that a simple dietary supplement could provide another way to manage symptoms.

"This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change -- adding a fiber supplement to your breakfast or yogurt -- could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function," said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki, lead author of the study from the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham.

The supplement tested in the study was inulin, a naturally occurring fiber found in foods such as chicory root, Jerusalem artichokes, and certain other vegetables. Unlike many nutrients, inulin is not broken down by digestive enzymes in the small intestine. Instead, it passes into the large intestine, where beneficial bacteria can use it as food.

How Gut Bacteria May Influence Arthritis Pain

Researchers are increasingly discovering that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influences much more than digestion. These microbes interact with the immune system, produce biologically active compounds, and may even affect how the nervous system responds to pain.

Inulin is classified as a prebiotic because it nourishes certain beneficial gut bacteria rather than directly supplying living microorganisms, as probiotics do.

When bacteria ferment inulin, they produce substances known as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). One of the most important is butyrate, a compound that helps support the intestinal lining and can influence inflammation and biological pathways involved in pain.

The researchers found that participants taking inulin had increased levels of butyrate, suggesting that the supplement was influencing activity within the gut microbiome.

They also observed higher levels of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the gut that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite and has also been linked to pain regulation and muscle health.

GLP-1 has attracted widespread attention because it is the hormone targeted by medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. However, the inulin supplement used in this trial was not a GLP-1 medication. Instead, researchers examined whether supporting beneficial gut bacteria could influence the body's own production of the hormone.

One particularly interesting finding was that higher GLP-1 levels were associated with better grip strength. Although this does not establish that GLP-1 caused the improvement, it suggests that changes originating in the digestive system may be connected to muscle function as well as pain.

To investigate these effects, the researchers conducted the INSPIRE trial, a six-week randomized controlled study involving 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis.

Participants were assigned to one of four treatment groups: a daily inulin supplement alone, digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE) alone, a combination of inulin and physical therapy, or a placebo.

This design allowed researchers to examine the effects of the supplement and exercise separately, as well as investigate whether combining them offered additional benefits.

Both inulin and physical therapy independently reduced knee pain, indicating that each approach provided meaningful symptom relief.

However, the supplement produced additional improvements that were not observed with physical therapy alone. Participants taking inulin demonstrated better grip strength and reduced pain sensitivity.

Pain sensitivity reflects how strongly the nervous system responds to potentially painful stimulation. Reducing that sensitivity could be particularly valuable for people with osteoarthritis, because persistent pain is not always explained by the amount of visible damage within a joint. Changes in how the nervous system processes pain can also contribute to discomfort.

The improved grip strength was another unexpected result, suggesting that the supplement's effects might extend beyond the knee itself.

The researchers also found a substantial difference in how many participants completed their assigned treatments. Only 3.6% of the inulin-only group dropped out, compared with 21% of the physical therapy-only group.

This difference suggests that taking a daily fiber supplement may be easier to incorporate into a regular routine than following a structured exercise program.

A Surprising Connection Between Gut Health, Muscles, and Pain

Dr. Kouraki said: "Our findings suggest that targeting gut health with a prebiotic supplement is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective way to reduce pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. The very low dropout rate compared to the exercise group is also encouraging from a public health perspective -- people were able to fit this supplement easily into their daily lives."

Beyond the reduction in arthritis pain, the researchers are particularly interested in what the findings reveal about interactions between the digestive system, muscles, and nervous system.

The association between GLP-1 and grip strength raises the possibility of a broader biological relationship connecting gut health with physical performance and resilience as people age.

Senior author Professor Ana Valdes from the School of Medicine added: "The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation. This could have implications not just for osteoarthritis, but for understanding how gut health influences aging and physical resilience more broadly."

The findings are promising, but the trial was relatively small and lasted only six weeks. Larger studies with longer follow-up periods will be needed to establish whether the benefits persist, identify which patients are most likely to respond, and clarify the biological mechanisms responsible.

The results also do not suggest that fiber supplements should replace exercise or other established arthritis treatments. Instead, they point toward a potentially useful additional approach that could complement existing care.

The potential importance of this research becomes clearer when considering how many people live with persistent arthritis pain.

Professor Lucy Donaldson, Director of Research at Arthritis UK, said: "The pain of arthritis can severely impact quality of life. Our recent lived experience survey showed that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis.

"Researchers are starting to explore the role of the gut microbiome in our experience of pain. This exciting preliminary research highlights how diet and physiotherapy can act in different ways to have benefits for people with arthritis. We know a variety and balance of healthy foods, including fiber, and regular physical activity matter, and we're glad to be supporting research that explores how they work to help people with arthritis."

For people living with knee osteoarthritis, the findings offer an encouraging possibility: a relatively simple change in daily nutrition may help reduce pain while supporting other aspects of physical health.

Perhaps most intriguingly, the research suggests that treating arthritis may involve looking beyond the joints themselves. By exploring how gut bacteria influence inflammation, pain perception, and muscle function, scientists may uncover new ways to manage a condition that affects millions of people every day.

#5728. The Renovation Cool-Off Is Here, but Delaying Certain Repairs Could Cost You More Than You Save

Spending on home improvements and repairs is only expected to grow by 1.5% by the third quarter of 2027, according to Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies. Given the high cost of labor and materials these days, this is no surprise.

But if you’re trying to cut back on home projects to save some cash, it's important to understand which ones are truly optional and which ones actually need immediate attention.

“Not every project needs to happen right away. Your home doesn't have to look brand-new to be safe, comfortable, and in good shape,” says Jeri Goodkin Dausey, president and certified general contractor at SBC in Miami Beach, FL.

By knowing how to prioritze your budget, you can protect your home’s condition and value without draining your savings.

There are quite a few projects you can delay without hurting your home, as long as everything is safe and working properly.

“Sometimes, waiting can save you quite a bit of money in the short term,” Dausey explains.

Here’s what you can put on the back burner until you have more funds at your disposal.

If your cabinets, countertops, and fixtures are still in decent shape and everything works, there's no need to rush into a complete remodel.

“Let's say you were planning to spend $25,000 on a renovation but could take care of the immediate issue with a $500 repair instead. That's $24,500 you can hold onto for now,” says Dausey.

A fresh coat of paint or new trim can make a significant difference in your home’s aestehtics, but these are usually things that can wait if the walls and surfaces are in good shape.

“If you put off a $4,000 paint job and just spend $200 on a few touch-ups, you've kept another $3,800 in your budget,” Dausey explains.

Dmitri Popescu, general manager at Olympic Decks in Seattle, echoes Dausey’s thoughts.

“Repainting a room because you dislike the color or replacing an undamaged backsplash can generally wait. There’s no need to spend your money on a temporary makeover,” Popescu explains.

Not loving the look of your floors doesn't necessarily mean you need to replace them. If they're safe, stable, and free of water damage, you may be able to live with them a little longer.

“Putting off an $8,000 replacement and spending $300 on maintenance leaves you with $7,700. Just be sure to check out loose tiles, soft spots or areas that are lifting,” says Dausey.

An outdoor kitchen, new landscaping, or a bigger patio might be nice to have, but they're not necessities. If everything outside is safe and in good shape, these projects can wait.

“Delaying a $15,000 cosmetic upgrade in your backyard frees up a lot of money for other things. Just don't overlook problems like poor drainage, hazardous trees, or an unsafe deck,” advises Dausey.

These expert tips can help you decide whether a project can wait:

Ask yourself, does this project actually protect my home, or is it simply for aesthetics?

“Cosmetic upgrades can wait, but projects that protect the structural integrity and long-term value of your property can't,” says Roxanne Conrad, chief operating officer at Premium Service Brands in Charlottesville, VA.

Clogged gutters and unstable exterior surfaces like missing shingles and unsealed windows, for example, can be an issue.

“They can lead to much larger problems down the road if neglected for too long,” Conrad says.

If you’ve noticed the issue a while ago and it’s worsening, it likely deserves your time and money.

“Catching problems early is almost always easier and cheaper than repairing them as they fail,” Conrad explains.

Take care of what keeps your home safe, dry, and in good shape, and don't feel pressured to tackle every cosmetic project right away.

Keith Ostendorf, project developer at Next Stage Design + Build in San Jose, CA, recommends phasing.

“Some homeowners move forward in phases, which spreads out the spending and can cut the costs of moving out, since work in one part of the house can happen while the family lives in the rest,” he adds.

#5727. A single sauna session sends immune cells surging through your body

A single sauna session may trigger a surprising response in the immune system. Researchers in Finland have discovered that spending just 30 minutes in a sauna, with a brief cold shower halfway through, causes white blood cells to surge into the bloodstream. These cells are essential to the body's defenses, helping identify and fight infections and other potential threats.

The findings suggest that sauna bathing may temporarily mobilize immune cells that normally remain in tissues, allowing them to circulate more widely throughout the body. This increased movement could help the immune system monitor for harmful pathogens, including bacteria and viruses.

During the study, researchers observed an increase in every type of circulating white blood cell they measured. Among them were neutrophils and lymphocytes, two important groups of immune cells. Neutrophils are often among the first defenders to respond to an infection, while lymphocytes include cells that recognize specific threats, produce antibodies, and help coordinate immune responses.

The increase was temporary. Within 30 minutes after the sauna session, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts had returned to their original levels.

How Sauna Bathing May Activate Immune Defenses

"This may indicate that sauna bathing mobilizes additional white blood cells into the bloodstream from tissues, where they are then redeposited after the session. This kind of periodic release of white blood cells into the bloodstream is beneficial, as once they leave their storage sites, they are better able to patrol the body and respond to pathogens," says Ilkka Heinonen, an Academy Research Fellow at the University of Turku.

This process is known as immune surveillance. Rather than remaining in one location, immune cells travel through the bloodstream and tissues, searching for signs of infection or other abnormalities. By temporarily increasing the number of white blood cells in circulation, the body may improve their ability to detect potential threats.

Interestingly, a similar response occurs during physical exercise. Exercise can temporarily increase the number of immune cells moving through the bloodstream, helping distribute them throughout the body. The new findings suggest that sauna bathing may produce a comparable short-term response, although this does not mean the two activities provide identical immune benefits.

Sauna Heat Also Affects Immune Signaling Molecules

The researchers also investigated whether sauna bathing influenced cytokines, small proteins that help immune cells communicate with one another. Cytokines play important roles in regulating inflammation, coordinating immune defenses, and directing the body's response to infections.

Overall, the sauna session produced little change in average cytokine levels in the bloodstream. However, a closer examination revealed an interesting connection between certain cytokines and changes in body temperature.

"Interestingly, however, the levels of several cytokines changed in relation to how much body temperature rose during sauna bathing. No similar association was observed between white blood cell counts and changes in body temperature," says Professor Jari Laukkanen, who led the study at the University of Eastern Finland.

In other words, some immune signaling molecules responded differently depending on how much a person's body temperature increased. White blood cell counts, however, did not show the same relationship with rising body temperature.

This distinction suggests that sauna bathing may influence different parts of the immune system through different physiological processes.

What This Discovery Means for Sauna Health Benefits

Previous research has linked regular sauna bathing with several potential health benefits. The latest findings offer another clue about what may be happening inside the body during these sessions, particularly how heat exposure and the sauna routine affect immune cell circulation.

However, the researchers caution that the results do not establish whether sauna bathing produces lasting improvements in immune function or reduces the risk of illness. The study examined only the immediate effects of one sauna session, and the observed changes in white blood cells were short-lived.

Because the session also included a brief cold shower, the findings reflect the combined sauna and cooling routine rather than the isolated effects of heat alone.

The research involved 51 adults with an average age of 50. The findings were published in the scientific journal Temperature, which specializes in research on body temperature regulation and its effects on human physiology.

Although more research is needed to understand the long-term implications, the study reveals that even a single sauna session can rapidly change how immune cells circulate through the body, potentially offering new insight into the biological effects of this popular relaxation practice.

#5726. Most people haven’t heard of kratom. What is it, and who’s using it?

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Theresa covers substance use and addiction and co-writes the Morning Rounds newsletter. You can reach Theresa on Signal at theresagaff.97.

Over the last few years, the kratom plant and supplements made from it have garnered increasing attention from public health leaders. This broad category of products, which largely skirts any regulation, has seen major surges in potency, while becoming omnipresent on smoke shop and gas station shelves. Health officials have warned that concentrated compounds like 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) are an emerging public health threat, and federal policies to limit their availability are pending. In the meantime, multiple states and smaller localities have issued emergency bans on 7-OH, and in some cases, on all kratom products.

Despite the messaging and rising use, few Americans are familiar with kratom or the newer derivative products. They’re made with compounds that have scientific names like 7-OH, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI) and dihydro-7-hydroxy mitragynine (MGM-15) but are often sold on shelves with names like Dozo Perks, Roxy, and UltraOhmz Pseudo Supreme. New survey data from the Annenberg Public Policy Center show about two-thirds (66%) of Americans have never heard of kratom. Among those who had at least some familiarity, few understood the difference between its natural leaf form and more synthetic products.

That confusion carries over to the associated risks. In the survey of nearly 2,000 people, 66% were unsure if kratom products posed a serious public safety hazard. And most people didn’t understand health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s stance on regulation — a question that’s become complicated by repeated reports of kratom industry lobbying influence on the DEA’s proposed action.

STAT spoke with researchers and people who use or have used kratom and 7-OH to get a full picture of what these products are, along with their potential risks and benefits.

To an untrained eye, a kratom leaf might resemble a bay leaf. It grows on evergreen trees indigenous to Southeast Asian countries, including Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. For centuries, people there have chewed the leaf or brewed it into tea for its stimulant-like effects.

Kratom (pronounce it with a hard or soft “a,” your choice) contains dozens of alkaloids, but mitragynine is the most abundant and the best understood. It acts as a partial agonist that binds to mu-opioid receptors in the nervous system. (Partial agonists produce less of a response from the receptor than full agonists, such as fentanyl or oxycodone.)

The first kratom products to arrive in the U.S. were made by drying and grinding up those leaves to create a matcha-like powder often used as a tea or swallowed in a capsule. In low quantities, it acts as a mild stimulant that can appear similar to coffee. In higher doses, people have used kratom to stave off chronic pain and even to help ease withdrawal from opioids. (There are no evidence-based dose recommendations, and there’s a lot of variation in both product potency and personal preference.)

“We call it swamp water, so that should give you a good visual,” said Madalyn Sklar, who uses kratom to ease chronic pain caused by degenerative disc disease, and hosts two podcasts on kratom. The first time Sklar drank the bitter tea made from kratom powder, she added orange juice as a sweetener, but still “it was so gross that I almost puked.” She’s taken it nearly every day since 2019, and says the results are better than when she was on meds like OxyContin and gabapentin.

She takes two teaspoons of powder — which works out to about 70-75 milligrams of mitragynine — every six hours. For her, there’s no high or euphoria. But she can do simple tasks that she couldn’t before, such as walk her dog and bend down to pick up its poop.

Sklar hasn’t experienced withdrawal symptoms when she’s occasionally stopped taking kratom and returned to more traditional pain medication. Research is limited, but has found that up to around 38% of kratom users may develop use disorders. In studies, withdrawal from kratom has appeared mild on a scale that measures clinical opioid withdrawal, with symptoms like anxiety, fatigue, gastrointestinal issues, and restlessness.

Before semi-synthetic products came onto the scene, most public health concern around kratom was directed at extracts and tinctures, recalled Sklar. Many of these products still tout mitragynine as the active ingredient, but in much more concentrated volumes than the whole leaf powder — think 100 to 300 milligrams of mitragynine in a bottle of liquid the size of a 5-hour Energy. (There are currently no federal proposals that aim to regulate concentrated mitragynine products.)

“But people got really interested in the other alkaloids over time,” said Katherine Hill, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health who has studied kratom. “And specifically they got interested in 7-hydroxymitrogynine.”

The alkaloid 7-OH does not appear in the fresh kratom leaf that people in Southeast Asia chew, according to Hill. It shows up in the dried leaf powder products, in small amounts. It’s also a metabolite, meaning that when the body absorbs mitragynine, some of it turns it into 7-OH. Once inside the body, 7-OH, like mitragynine, is a partial agonist to the mu-opioid receptor.

The products made with 7-OH — including tablets, gummies, shots, and drink powders — are semi-synthetic; they contain artificially concentrated amounts of the compound. When the products first started popping up, they were often sold in tablets containing 12-14 milligrams, users said. Those can offer sedative effects and pain relief. But now, tablets containing 25, 50, and even 100 milligrams of 7-OH are available.

“The first time I heard of 7-OH, it was very negative,” said Twinkle VanFleet, who co-hosts a kratom podcast with Sklar.

While natural kratom products carry a risk of dependence and what’s thought to be mild withdrawal at low doses, there’s growing concern that concentrated 7-OH products are even more addictive, and that withdrawal can be as bad as coming off a traditional opioid. Hill is working on a study of 7-OH users that will look at both tolerance and withdrawal. But for now, the risks are mainly documented in case reports, series, and other anecdotal accounts.

VanFleet suffers from intense pain from an injury that led to complex regional pain syndrome, and she has a deep mistrust of the medical system. Kratom didn’t ease her symptoms, so she eventually tried 7-OH, and found comfort in what she calls “nibbles” of smaller tablets. She currently takes around 12 milligrams per day and worries about a ban by the Drug Enforcement Administration. Still, she shares concerns about the availability of higher-dose products.

“I do see both sides of a lot of this,” VanFleet said. “In my perfect world, there would be 3, 5, and 10 milligram tablets, period. If even that.”

Greg Kiesow had been sober from alcohol for nearly 20 years and retired for three days when he went into a smoke shop that was promoting 7-OH products. The shopkeeper had heard it was some sort of natural energy supplement, like coffee, and gave Kiesow a free sample of tablets. “I took it home, and I took it. And 10 to 15 minutes later, it wasn’t coffee. It was a very powerful opioid,” Kiesow said.

Kiesow said he quickly developed an addiction. After 10 months, which he described as an extremely isolated period spent sitting on his back porch watching the birds at his bird feeder, he began to taper himself off the products. A few weeks later, he formed Kratom Anonymous, which has 15 virtual meetings per week for people looking to quit.

As 7-OH gained popularity, newer synthetic products have continued to crop up, including some with concentrated levels of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI), another metabolite of mitragynine. Over the summer, the DEA proposed a ban of MGPI at any quantity. But an updated proposal in October, pushed by a lobbyist for the American Kratom Association, would allow small amounts of the compound to show up in products. Instead of an outright ban, the DEA now proposes limiting both MGPI and 7-OH based on the ratio of those compounds to mitragynine in any given product.

The reason for the change, according to the DEA, is that trace amounts of MGPI could appear in natural kratom. But the safety of small amounts is unclear. Test results presented in recent wrongful death lawsuits suggest that a natural kratom powder product, used by somebody who died after taking it, was likely contaminated with MGPI.

As more people use kratom and other associated products, there’s a growing recognition of the potential risk for addiction. Over 10 years, the National Poison Data Center found a 1,200% increase in kratom-related exposure reports — from 258 in 2015 to 3,434 in 2025. That includes all types of products. Clinicians who run addiction treatment centers say, over the last year, they’ve seen a rise in patients seeking help to get off 7-OH in particular.

But data on the most serious risks — overdose and death — are murky. The poison center data showed 233 deaths over the decade, most of which involved other substances like opioids, benzodiazepines, stimulants, and alcohol. (Researchers believe kratom can exacerbate the danger of a drug like fentanyl, and even more common medications like certain antidepressants.) A 2023 investigation by the Tampa Bay Times found that, over nearly 10 years, more than 580 people in Florida alone died from overdoses that involved kratom products.

Because both 7-OH and MGPI are metabolites of mitragynine, it can be difficult to draw conclusions about a given death, even with toxicology data. Complicating the matter even further: When tested, many kratom products — natural and synthetic — are found to have different concentration levels than the labels advertise, and some have been found to contain compounds that were not on the label at all.

Sklar and VanFleet are both proponents of regulations, not bans, on all types of kratom-related products. Others who advocate for natural kratom are working hard to distance themselves from the more synthetic products.

“Any who unwittingly support every concentrated 7-OH product are not defending the natural kratom plant. It may be helping to destroy it,” Mac Haddow, the American Kratom Association’s lobbyist, said in a recent video. “The solution is not to defend everything. The solution is to draw a clear, bright line.”

But others said they’ve suffered from taking natural kratom products, too. Danelle Kawasaki first tried kratom at a dry bar in her Montana town. It came at room temperature, and was advertised as a natural, herbal tea. The concoction eased her anxiety, making her feel both calm and energetic, able to speak with anyone she wanted. At first it was a weekly treat, then a few times a week. After a few months, she was having two drinks per day. She’d wake up with a jolt of anxiety, which she attributes to the tea not being in her system overnight. Without more, she’d be sick, crawling to the bathroom to puke.

It frustrates Kawasaki when people try to tell her that 7-OH, not natural kratom, is the problem. “This argument comes up all the time and it drives me nuts,” she said. “I know what was going on — it was the actual kratom tea powder. It wasn’t a concentrated form.”

At one point, she was drinking nearly 140 ounces of the tea per day. When she finally stopped, cold turkey, the withdrawal was its own dayslong nightmare.

Now, she advocates that the Fort Peck tribe, of which she’s a member, ban kratom on the reservation. For Kawasaki, “the risks outweigh the remedy that people are searching for.”

#5725. Opinion: AI depends on medical records that don’t always tell the full truth about women

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Annemarie G. Hirsch and Jennifer Silva

Hirsch and Silva are authors of “Seen But Not Heard: What Medical Records Don’t Tell Us About Women’s Lives.”

In September, the Gallup-Pivotal Women’s Health Survey reported that 34% of U.S. women strongly or somewhat agreed that a health care provider minimized or dismissed their symptoms in the past five years. Thirty-three percent reported being misdiagnosed or unable to get a diagnosis, compared with 21% of men reporting these experiences.

Medical records tell a different story. An epidemiologist and a sociologist, we recently released a study where we paired electronic medical records with detailed interviews with 87 women. We talked to these women about their pain and illnesses, work, family, poverty, violence, and encounters with the health care system.

Fifty-three of the women described a trust-breaking encounter with a health system, but only seven of them had medical records that documented mistrust. Thirty-two women reported experiencing a misdiagnosis, but misdiagnosis was only documented for eight of these women. Thirty women reported that they felt that clinicians treated them with disrespect, but this was not documented in the records anywhere.

For more than a decade, Kate lived with debilitating pelvic pain. Her doctors repeatedly attributed her symptoms to obesity. Her medical record reflected these assumptions.

When Kate underwent bariatric surgery and lost a significant amount of weight, her clinical notes became optimistic.

However, her symptoms persisted. Medical records pivoted from linking symptoms from obesity to mental health factors.

“Gastrointestinal malfunctions arising from mental factors.”

The turning point came only after Kate attended an appointment with her new husband. In the clinical notes, the provider documented Kate’s husband’s concerns:

For the first time in 10 years, doctors conducted the exams needed to finally diagnose Kate with endometriosis.

Kate’s medical record accurately documented years of conversations about weight and mental health. What it failed to capture was equally important: the cost of years spent with an undiagnosed disease, the frustration of not being believed, and the erosion of trust that occurs when symptoms are repeatedly explained away rather than investigated. Kate told us, “If I was tired, it was because I was overweight. If I had cramps, it was because I was overweight. Migraines, I was overweight. … They’re not hearing what you’re saying, and that compounded the issues that were going on.”

We often think of medical records as objective accounts of a patient’s health. They are not. Medical records are narratives, shaped by the questions clinicians ask and the assumptions they bring into the room. Medical record data reflect clinical decisions as well as biology. The language clinicians use and the details they choose to record can reinforce stereotypes that follow patients from one encounter to the next, influencing how future clinicians interpret symptoms, assess credibility, and make treatment decisions.

Medical record data also reflect what patients feel comfortable disclosing. What women share with their doctors depends on how much they trust them and how safe they feel. When people fear judgment, dismissal, or not being believed, important parts of their stories may remain unspoken, and thus, undocumented.

This fear may why 53 women in our data described a trust-breaking clinical encounter in their interview, while only seven of their medical records noted their mistrust. This is particularly a problem for women, who feel the pressure to be pleasant and pliant with doctors for fear of not being taken seriously.

Across the country, clinics and hospitals are adopting AI scribes that transcribe recorded interactions between doctor and patient and produce a clinical note. AI tools can be used to search and synthesize medical records to help with diagnostics and treatment plans, some with great success.

However, these tools are only as good as the data in the medical record. If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.

For AI to achieve its full potential in women’s health, medical records need to tell the complete story. Health care settings must be safe spaces where women can tell their stories; clinicians need to listen to women, even when their experiences do not fit clinical expectations; and clinicians need to document in the medical record when diagnoses are delayed or incorrect, without fear of being penalized.

Armed with these data, AI has the potential to do more than replicate biases of the past. AI could help identify patterns of missed diagnoses, reduce disparities in care, and ensure that more women are heard.

Annemarie G. Hirsch, Ph.D., M.P.H., and Jennifer Silva, Ph.D., are authors of “Seen But Not Heard: What Medical Records Don’t Tell Us About Women’s Lives.”

#5723. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5722. A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms

Scientists have identified a brain signal that may help explain why schizophrenia produces such a wide variety of symptoms, including difficulties with perception, movement, and speech. The discovery suggests that problems that appear unrelated could actually stem from a shared disruption in how the brain processes information.

Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder that can affect how people experience the world, interact with their surroundings, and communicate with others. These symptoms are typically studied as separate features of the condition, but new research suggests they may have more in common than previously recognized.

The study, published in Science Advances, was conducted by scientists from McGill University, the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, the University of Montreal, the Research Centre of the University of Montreal Health Centre, and the Douglas Research Centre. Their findings point to a common brain mechanism that may help explain several distinct symptoms of schizophrenia.

A Weakened Brain Signal Links Multiple Schizophrenia Symptoms

To investigate this connection, researchers examined beta-band brain activity in 25 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants. Beta-band activity refers to rhythmic patterns of electrical activity in the brain that are involved in coordinating information processing, perception, and movement.

Participants completed tasks designed to test how accurately they could judge the timing of visual and auditory information. The researchers also analyzed their speech to look for signs of disorganized thinking and communication.

The results revealed a striking pattern. People with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity than those in the control group. More importantly, the participants with the most pronounced abnormalities in this brain signal also tended to have greater difficulty processing the timing of sights and sounds, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.

These three features of schizophrenia are usually investigated independently. Finding that they were all associated with changes in the same brain signal suggests that a shared underlying process may contribute to the disorder's diverse effects.

A New Window Into How the Brain Processes Reality

"This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain's operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia," said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.

The brain constantly uses incoming sensory information to develop and update its understanding of the surrounding environment. This process helps people interpret what they see and hear, anticipate events, and coordinate their actions. The new findings suggest that disruptions in this process could help explain why schizophrenia affects several different aspects of behavior and perception.

The researchers used high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to measure brain activity. This imaging technique detects the tiny magnetic fields generated by electrical activity in the brain, allowing scientists to track changes in neural signals with exceptional precision. The scans were performed at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro).

"What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement," said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and postdoctoral scholar in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre. "Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms."

Could the Discovery Help Detect Psychosis Earlier?

Beyond providing new insight into schizophrenia, the findings could eventually help researchers identify young people who are at greater risk of developing psychosis. Psychosis involves a disruption in how someone perceives or interprets reality and can include experiences such as hallucinations or delusions.

Early identification is particularly important because the first signs of schizophrenia often appear during adolescence but may go unrecognized for an extended period.

"The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis," Palaniyappan said.

However, the researchers emphasized that the results are preliminary. The study included only 50 participants, and additional research involving larger, independent groups will be necessary to determine how reliably the brain signal is associated with speech disturbances and overall symptom severity.

"This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them," Wei said.

If future studies confirm the findings, measuring beta-band activity could potentially become a useful tool for identifying people who need earlier support. Wei also suggested that the brain signal may deserve investigation as a possible target for future schizophrenia treatments.

Medicare regulators this week pushed forward with a controversial plan to ban hospitals and other providers from using third parties to deliver remote patient monitoring services, despite overwhelming opposition from health tech companies, hospitals, insurers, and specialty organizations.

#5720. Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress

Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January.

The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed.

The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump, who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence."

Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.

"If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula, CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com.

Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas, Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend.

Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in.

Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act.

That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts. But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level.

In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act, with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines.

Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move.

Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence.

The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding."

While data centers affect property taxes, the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open.

Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers.

"Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far."

The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions.

Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas.

It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says.

"That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5719. Scientists discover that cranberry juice may help fight tooth decay

Cranberry juice may offer an unexpected benefit for your teeth. New research suggests that pure, unsweetened cranberry juice can slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay.

Cranberries are a familiar part of holiday celebrations. They appear in sauces, salads, and cocktails, and even serve as colorful seasonal decorations. But beyond their tart flavor and festive appeal, these small red berries contain natural compounds that may support oral health.

Christine Wu, a researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, has been investigating whether cranberry juice could help protect teeth from harmful bacteria. Her findings suggest that the popular beverage may have benefits that go beyond its traditional association with urinary tract health.

How Cranberry Juice Affects Harmful Bacteria

Cranberry juice has long been used to help prevent urinary tract infections. One reason is that cranberries contain compounds called proanthocyanidins, which have anti-inflammatory properties and can interfere with the ability of certain bacteria, including E. coli, to attach to cells.

Wu wanted to determine whether these same compounds might also affect bacteria found in dental plaque. These microorganisms feed on sugars from food and drinks, producing acids that gradually weaken tooth enamel and contribute to cavities.

Rather than testing isolated cranberry compounds, Wu chose to investigate pure cranberry juice, a product people can readily purchase and consume.

"Just like sugar damage is linked to diet, I'm interested in how the food and beverages we consume can help combat the harmful bacteria and benefit our oral health," Wu said.

To investigate the potential effects, researchers conducted a small human study involving 22 participants, including 14 children and eight adults.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three beverages: pure, unsweetened 100% cranberry juice, a cranberry juice cocktail containing 27% juice and added sugar, or plain water.

"It was important to us to conduct these tests with human participants and use products available on the market. Most cranberry juice studies have been conducted using laboratory-prepared cranberry juice extract. Moreover, limited studies have been performed in children," said Wu, who is a professor of pediatric dentistry.

On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived with dental plaque that had accumulated overnight. Researchers first collected plaque samples using cotton swabs on one side of each participant's mouth.

After rinsing with water, participants consumed three small amounts of their assigned beverage. They swished each drink around their mouths several times before swallowing.

Thirty minutes later, researchers collected another set of plaque samples, this time from teeth that had not been swabbed earlier. Comparing the samples allowed the team to examine how each beverage affected plaque activity over the short testing period.

A Surprising Effect on Plaque and Tooth Decay

The results revealed a promising effect of pure cranberry juice. Dental plaque exposed to the unsweetened beverage showed slower regrowth than unexposed plaque samples.

Researchers also found that swishing with pure cranberry juice reduced acid production in dental plaque from both children and adults. This is particularly important because acids produced by oral bacteria can gradually erode tooth enamel, increasing the risk of cavities.

The findings suggest that cranberry juice may interfere with two important processes involved in tooth decay: the buildup of bacterial plaque and the production of damaging acids.

Wu believes these results could eventually support the development of cranberry juice as a "functional beverage" that offers benefits for oral health. The findings are especially interesting because other commonly consumed fruit juices, including orange and apple juice, have not shown the same promise in this research context.

"Most people think of cranberry juice as very sour, very acidic and sugary, and therefore may not contribute positively to oral health. This study found the opposite: that cranberry juice affected dental plaque regrowth and acid production, which may counteract some of the damage done by sugar," she said.

Could Cranberry Juice Become Part of Oral Care?

Although the findings are encouraging, the researchers emphasize that further investigation is necessary. With only 22 participants and a testing period lasting just 30 minutes after consumption, the study cannot establish whether drinking cranberry juice regularly prevents cavities or produces lasting improvements in dental health.

Larger studies conducted over longer periods will be needed to determine whether the observed changes in dental plaque translate into meaningful protection against tooth decay.

Still, Wu sees potential in occasionally using pure cranberry juice as a mouth rinse. One challenge is its intensely tart flavor, which some people may find unpleasant without added sweetness.

"But maybe by adding an appropriate sugar substitute," she said, "to make it a bit more palatable."

The research was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#5717. Zillow Says Lawsuits in the Past, ‘Not Obvious’ How Market Recovers

Real estate’s biggest name is struggling, just like everyone else, but company leadership is promising that it—and the industry—have ways to hang on amid a tech revolution, a sluggish market and legal woes the company claims are in the past now.

Speaking to investors after reporting earnings for Q3 2026, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business,” with CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann adding that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

Zillow’s report comes as mortgage rates remain elevated from earlier this year and existing home sales are on track to come in around 4 million—down more than 20% from pre-pandemic norms. The company’s stock fell sharply, down around 17% in after-hours trading.

The company still faces a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Democratic lawmakers previously offered pointed criticism of some of Zillow’s business practices, which are also used by at least some other portals, as the party made big gains in the midterms yesterday.

On the tech side, Zillow said it has not seen major impacts from increased use of AI by consumers, or Google’s ongoing push into residential real estate.

“(Google’s program) is very different than a ‘Preferred’ connection and an integrated transaction and helping agents grow their business that way. So we haven’t seen any impact from it today, even though it’s supposedly live nationwide,” Wacksman said.

As the company previously announced, agent partners are all being transitioned from other programs to the company’s Zillow Preferred service, which executives said is integrated with Zillow Home Loans.

The transition is expected to be fully implemented by the first half of 2027, and 75% complete by the end of this year.

Zillow’s residential for-sale revenue was down 4% year-over-year, $419 million in Q3 2026 compared to $435 million in Q3 2025. On the other hand, mortgage revenue grew 32%, and the company touted durable rental income, up 26% from the same period last year.

Overall revenue came in up 7% from last year at $724 million, with the lawsuit payment—$165 million after insurance covered part of the settlement—dinging the top—line. Outlook for Q4—historically the slowest for real estate—was $635 to $665 million, roughly the same as last year’s reported $654 million.

Late last year, Zillow was targeted by a high-profile class-action firm with claims from recent homebuyers focused on those “lead diversion” and loan referral practices. A judge initially threw that lawsuit out (though plaintiffs are seeking to revive it).

The company also agreed last week to pay $212.5 million to settle a lawsuit over its long-shuttered iBuying business, something the company said it was happy to put behind it.

“I think we’ve been pretty consistent and transparent to the degree we could be, that we didn’t expect these cases to impact business. And I think as you’re seeing them resolve, get settled, move on, you’re seeing that come to light. They’re not impacting our business,” Wacksman said.

As far as the macro picture, Hofmann said that without any sign of a market rebound, “its our job (to) just keep driving on the underlying structural growth drivers we have,” including software and rentals that are not rate dependent.

“We’re also fortunate in that the business has diversified pretty rapidly over the last four or five years,” he said.

Addressing the use of agentic AI and potential changes in how consumers search for homes, Wacksman and Hofmann both promised that Zillow’s model was built to thrive in this new environment.

“We see the human experiences remaining human,” Wacksman said. “The dreaming and shopping part is the part you want to do and the transaction part is the part you need to do, and Zillow is the best place to do both those things…and then our ability to make the professional’s job easier so they can serve the customer better is where we’re focused, and why we are so confident in the strategy.”

#5715. Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self

The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

Sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

The researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

The findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

The team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

When movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other important patterns:

Together, these findings provide new evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain

During ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

"In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," said corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are."

The findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

For someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain."

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

"Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity."

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

Both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan said. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life."

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

Mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

Zeidan's laboratory is currently conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

Although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

Funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

#5714. NYC Votes To Cut Construction Red Tape in Bid To Spur More Homebuilding

New York City voters overwhelmingly approved a plan to overhaul the city's notoriously complicated construction permitting process on Tuesday, handing Mayor Zohran Mamdani a victory in his effort to accelerate housing development.

Question 4, 1 of 5 ballot measures approved in the Nov. 3 election, received roughly 68% support, according to preliminary election results.

The measure promises to simplify construction by bringing 40 types of permits and approvals currently handled by 18 separate government offices and agencies into one centralized digital system.

"New Yorkers voted for a government that moves as fast as they do," Mamdani said in a statement on Tuesday night. The reforms would "directly address the affordability crisis and help New Yorkers stay in the city they love."

However, the new system isn't required to launch until 2030. Even when it does, faster permitting will address only one of the many obstacles making housing so difficult and expensive to build in New York.

"No single reform will be a silver bullet for housing supply and affordability, especially in a city like New York," explains Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com®. "Instead, each pro-supply policy change is a baby step in the right direction. And these marginal gains will add up."

The Big Apple needs approximately 700,000 additional homes over the next decade to meet existing and future demand, according to an August 2026 draft assessment from the city's housing and planning departments.

Yet developers filed plans for just 8,064 multifamily units in the second quarter of 2026, in a stunning 52% decline from the previous quarter, according to the Real Estate Board of New York.

That amounts to less than half the 17,500 new homes the city needs to add each quarter—and they're only proposed units, not completed homes.

Centralizing permits could help close that gap by cutting down the time and cost builders are forced to spend navigating city bureaucracy.

"Streamlining approvals can make a huge difference," Krimmel says. "It might not be the flashiest reform, but when it comes to new construction, time is money."

And permitting takes a very, very long time in New York City.

Of the nearly five years it takes to build a typical 20-unit apartment building in the Big Apple, roughly 1.5 years are spent securing permits alone, according to a September 2026 study examining construction timelines across 60 U.S. cities.

Now compare that to similar projects in Raleigh, NC, or Phoenix, where it takes roughly two years from application to completion.

"In a city like New York City with high land acquisition costs and a complex regulatory environment, predictability in timelines and financing can be critical for ensuring new construction can pencil," Krimmel says.

Research suggests those time savings could translate into more homes.

Cutting approval times by 25% could have increased multifamily housing production in Los Angeles by 12.7% between 2010 and 2022, according to a 2026 study published in the Journal of Urban Economics.

When researchers accounted for additional development that faster approvals might encourage, the estimated increase reached 23.7%.

The question for New Yorkers, though, is when those reforms might translate into more housing options and lower rents. The median monthly asking rent hit $3,785 in October—up 4.5% from a year ago.

Under the new rules, applicants would have one digital portal to submit documents, track applications, and obtain approvals, rather than navigating separate systems across multiple agencies.

But streamlining applications doesn't necessarily mean they'll be reviewed any faster.

In fact, the average time required to approve applications through the Department of Buildings' existing digital portal climbed from 8.3 days in 2020 to 20.3 days in 2025, according to a July report from New York State Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli.

And its hardly the only challenge. Krimmel says the overhaul won't address other barriers to construction, including zoning restrictions and the complexity of financing multifamily developments.

Still, he sees the reform as one step toward untangling a much larger problem.

"In the same way that a complex web of red tape and veto points is extremely good at creating barriers to new construction, real solutions will require the city untangles that web bit by bit," he says.

With the new system potentially four years away, the first test will be whether it actually shortens permitting timelines. Any corresponding increase in housing construction—and relief for renters—could take considerably longer.

As Mamdani acknowledged on Tuesday night, "Now comes the work of turning these votes into results."

#5713. Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk

Could the amount of daylight you get each day offer clues about your risk of developing dementia? A large new study suggests that exposure to brighter daytime light is associated with a lower likelihood of developing the condition.

The findings, published in General Psychiatry, point to daytime light exposure as a potentially overlooked factor in brain health.

Brighter Daylight Linked to Lower Dementia Risk

To investigate the connection, researchers analyzed data from 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with accelerometers. The devices allowed scientists to measure participants' exposure to light during both the day and night. Over a median follow-up period of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia.

The results revealed a notable pattern. People exposed to average daytime light levels exceeding 1,000 lux (a moderately bright light level equivalent to an overcast day outdoors) had a 16% lower risk of developing dementia. Spending longer periods in even brighter daytime light (at least 5,000 lux) was associated with further reductions in risk.

Too Little Daylight Emerges as a Surprising Dementia Risk Indicator

One of the most striking findings involved people who received very little bright light during the day. Getting less than 0.7 hours, or 42 minutes, of bright daytime light daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than 6 established dementia risk factors.

Interestingly, researchers found no statistically significant connection between nighttime light exposure and dementia risk. This suggests that daytime brightness, rather than light exposure at night, may be particularly relevant to the relationship identified in the study.

"Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk," said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China.

Although the findings reveal an association, they do not establish that getting more daylight directly prevents dementia. Instead, the research highlights daytime light exposure as a potentially valuable indicator of dementia risk that deserves further investigation.

#5712. North Carolina Passes New Limits on Property Tax Levies

On Tuesday, North Carolina voters narrowly approved House Bill 1089, which proposed a limit on property tax increases. The amendment needed 60% of voters to support it to pass. It received 60.4% support.

The amendment does not specify the terms of those limits. Instead, that will be up to the North Carolina General Assembly to decide.

Proponents, including North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall, contended that surging property assessments have enabled local governments to impose excessive tax burdens on residents without delivering proportional public services.

Last year, Hall formed the House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform, a 23-member committee to examine property taxes in the state.

“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” Hall said in a press release earlier this year.

Support for the amendment fell across party lines. Conservatives and commercial organizations supported the measure, arguing that the amendment would help curb local government spending and protect property owners.

Political pundits theorized that the ballot measures were meant to entice Republican voters to the polls during an off-election year. But Western Carolina University professor Chris Cooper told NPR's All Things Considered the theory didn't hold much weight.

"The notion that North Carolinians were not going to show up and vote from the Republican persuasion, but now they are because of a constitutional amendment, is on there, frankly that stretches credibility for me a little bit."

But critics of the proposal said that creating a property tax cap would hobble local governments. Furthermore, the North Carolina Housing Coalition argued that the proposal would most benefit larger corporate property owners while providing little benefit to owners of single-family homes.

Tamika Walker Kelly, president of the North Carolina Association of Educators, criticized the bill for favoring “tax breaks over classrooms.”

“When local revenue is constrained, schools feel it immediately with overcrowded classrooms, aging school buildings, and educators stretched too thin,” Walker Kelly told NC Newsline. “A constitutional cap does not protect struggling families. It protects the largest landowners in the state, while the families who depend on public schools are left with less.”

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in North Carolina is 0.66%, which is relatively low compared with states such as New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.
