#5711. Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly

Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.

The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.

The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]

Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.

Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions

Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]

Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.

But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.

To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.

The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.

Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.

One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.

The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.

Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.

This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.

Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:

"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."

A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment

The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.

If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.

Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.

The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.

One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.

Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.

Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:

"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."

Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:

"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."

Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers

Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.

Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.

This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.

Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."

Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.

By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

#5710. Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

Materials provided by European Association for the Study of Diabetes. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5709. A $6.52 Million Beverlywood Home on a Lavish Golf Course Just Set the Record for the Priciest Teardown Sale

A Los Angeles property in Beverlywood has been sold in an off-market transaction, and at $6.52 million, it has set the record for the most expensive home to be purchased with plans to be torn down in the upscale neighborhood.

The dwelling is certainly in a coveted location, perched directly on the Hillcrest Country Club—a private club with an 18-hole golf course that has attracted celebrity members for more than a century.

According to Town and Country Magazine, the club’s initiation fee is a reported $185,000. Comedian Adam Sandler, singer-songwriter Neil Diamond, and Paramount co-founder Adolph Zukor are among the Hillcrest’s most notable members.

The home currently standing at 1807 Roxbury Drive is a three-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom abode spanning 2,874 square feet. It was built in 1953.

According to Micah Hiller of Prime Rock Realty, who represented the seller and buyer of 1807 Roxbury Drive, the new residents are looking to build a new house with a luxury construction company called Drexel Luxury Homes. They’d like a home with a much larger footprint.

The lot itself is 8,660 square feet, and Hiller estimates the buyers will be able to build a home that’s “at least” 4,500 square feet without a basement. Should they decide to add a lower ground floor, they’d likely be able to add an additional 2,000 or 3,000 square feet.

“This is the highest land-value sale in Beverlywood’s history,” Hiller tells Realtor.com®.

Hiller explains that Beverlywood has become a highly sought-after enclave, which, “despite the current market, continues to show incredible strength.”

“From what I’m seeing, demand for the neighborhood has only grown, and in some ways, it has become even more desirable than Beverly Hills,” he continues. “Buyers appreciate the community, location, and opportunity to create a home here.”

Beverlywood has seen some year-over-year softness in the housing market with the median listing price, price per square foot, and median days on the market all showing decreases from this time last year, according to Realtor.com data.

Still, each of these metrics is outperforming nationwide stats. In Beverlywood, the average listing is just under $2.4 million, while that number is just under $420,000 for the country as a whole.

Homes here also spend less than half the time on the market than they do nationwide, with Beverlywood listings being snapped up in an average of 29 days. The U.S. median is 61.

For the Los Angeles neighborhood, this number is down 21.62% year over year, signaling faster turnover and a more competitive environment for sellers.

As of October 2026, Beverlywood had an impressive sale-to-list price ratio of 99%, indicating a strong seller’s market for this desirable spot. There are also fewer opportunities for a buyer to find exactly what they’re looking for, as there are only a dozen active listings for sale.

Beverlywood is not the only corner of the country with a competitive market setting records.

In Provincetown, MA—where the price per square foot is six times the national median—the record for most-expensive condo sold was broken twice in a two-week period.

Thomas Andrews of Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty, who was the listing agent on both pricey transactions, said the vibrant community is the reason the local market is so coveted—which is quite similar to what Hiller says of Beverlywood.

“Provincetown is such a magical place. You have your Martha’s Vineyard, you have your Nantucket, but there’s so much soul in the creative arts in Provincetown that just makes it super vibrant and super sought-after,” he said.

Realtor.com senior economist Hannah Jones explains that the town has effectively reached its limit for new housing, which creates a tense battle for anyone who wants to find a home there.

"Provincetown sits at the very tip of Cape Cod, which means there is essentially no more space to build," she explains. "The housing stock is therefore relatively fixed, and any new supply has to come off from redevelopment or small-scale infill, both of which tend to be expensive and difficult to pull off."

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5708. Why the Garage Could Be a Home’s Biggest Flood Weak Spot

When homeowners think about protecting their property from flooding, the garage may not be the first place that comes to mind. But with its wide entrance, ground-level access and potential gaps around the door, a garage can be a vulnerable point when floodwater collects around a home.

A garage door’s bottom seal can help keep out everyday rain, leaves and debris, but it should not be assumed to provide reliable protection against floodwater. During periods of heavy rainfall, water may collect on a driveway, pool against the garage entrance or find its way through gaps around the door and threshold.

And the damage may not stop at a wet garage floor. Floodwater can affect vehicles, tools, appliances and stored belongings, while water entering through a connecting doorway may also threaten the rest of the house.

Cui Guanhong, flood barrier product specialist at Eudore, explains why homeowners should pay closer attention to their garages when preparing for flooding.

“Homeowners should consider the garage as part of their overall flood-prevention plan, rather than focusing only on front doors and windows,” he says. “The condition of the garage door seal, the height of the threshold and the way water moves across the driveway can all affect how vulnerable the entrance may be.”

Unlike a standard exterior door, a garage door often spans a wide opening close to ground level. This creates a larger area where water may enter if the door does not close properly or the surrounding surfaces allow water to accumulate.

“It’s worth checking what happens around the garage entrance during heavy rain,” says Cui. “If water consistently pools near the door, that is a sign to investigate the drainage and the way the driveway directs water.”

The bigger worry is often what is already inside the garage, starting with anything plugged in.

“The electrical risk comes first,” says Cui. “Outlets, extension cords, a chest freezer or a charger left plugged in can all become dangerous if floodwater reaches them.”

Official flood safety guidance from Ready.gov advises against touching electrical equipment if it is wet or if you are standing in water. Never enter a flooded garage or stand in water to reach electrical equipment or a breaker.

Garages may also contain water heaters and other heating equipment that could be damaged if floodwater reaches them. The extent of the damage depends on the equipment, its location and the depth of the water. Additionally, items stored at floor level, including power tools, paint cans, and cleaning products may be damaged or contaminated if floodwater enters the garage.

The connecting door is the part Cui believes homeowners underestimate most.

“If a garage opens directly into a hallway, laundry room, mudroom or kitchen, water entering the garage could potentially spread into the home,” he says. “Homeowners should consider this connection when assessing their property’s flood risk.”

Floor drains are the last detail, and the one that trips people up. During severe flooding, water may back up through floor drains if the drainage system becomes overwhelmed.

“Whether a backwater valve makes sense depends on how the property’s drainage is laid out, so that is a question for a qualified plumbing professional rather than a guess,” says Cui.

The best time to check your garage’s flood vulnerabilities is before a flood warning is issued. Waiting until water is already collecting outside the door may leave little time to inspect the entrance, install a barrier or move vulnerable belongings. Homeowners can start by checking their property’s flood risk, monitoring local weather alerts and preparing a plan for moving vehicles and important items to safer locations when necessary.

FEMA’s flood maps resources can help homeowners find official flood hazard information for their area, although a map should not be treated as a guarantee that a property will or will not flood.

It is also worth reviewing insurance arrangements before an emergency. Most standard homeowners insurance policies do not cover flood damage, so homeowners should check their policy and explore separate flood insurance if appropriate. FloodSmart, run by the National Flood Insurance Program, provides further information about flood insurance coverage and options.

Five ways to reduce a garage’s flood risk

Inspect the garage door seal. Check the bottom seal for cracks, gaps or signs of wear. Close the garage door and look for visible openings along the bottom and sides. Replace damaged seals in line with the manufacturer’s instructions. A sound seal can help limit ordinary water and debris entering through gaps, but it should not be treated as a substitute for flood protection.

Check the driveway and drainage. Observe where rainwater flows during a storm. Does it collect near the garage door, or does the driveway direct it towards the entrance? Keep drains and channels clear of leaves and debris. If water repeatedly pools around the garage, consider asking a qualified drainage or building professional to assess the slope and drainage arrangements. Any changes should be designed so they do not redirect water onto neighboring properties.

Consider a suitable flood barrier. Where flooding is a concern, a purpose-designed garage flood barrier may offer an additional layer of protection. However, not every barrier is suitable for every opening or flood scenario. Before choosing a product, check the dimensions of the garage entrance, the condition and level of the surfaces where the barrier will sit, and the manufacturer’s installation instructions and performance limitations. A barrier may be less effective if it is incorrectly fitted or used outside its specified conditions. Homeowners should also understand how quickly the barrier can be installed and where it will be stored so it can be accessed when needed.

Protect equipment and stored belongings. Where practical, keep valuable tools, electronics and important belongings off the garage floor. Use suitable shelving or storage that reduces the chance of items being damaged by shallow water. Store paints, fuels, cleaning products and other hazardous materials securely and in accordance with their labels. If electrical equipment, heating systems or other utilities could be exposed to floodwater, seek professional advice on appropriate protective measures.

Look at the route from the garage into your home. If your garage connects directly to your house, consider whether water entering the garage could reach the connecting doorway or adjoining rooms. The layout and floor levels of each property are different, so homeowners should avoid assuming that a simple DIY alteration will solve the problem. If flooding has affected the property before, a qualified building or flood-mitigation professional may be able to identify vulnerable entry points and appropriate improvements.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5707. Homebuilder Stocks Surge as Democratic Sweep Raises Hopes for Affordability Gains

Homebuilders and housing suppliers saw significant jumps in their share prices following the stunning success of Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

At the closing bell on Wednesday, shares of major builders Lennar and PulteGroup were up more than 7% on the day, and D.R. Horton rose more than 8%.

Suppliers showed similar increases. Home Depot finished the day up 6.5%, after spiking as much as 17% during midday trading, according to Yahoo Finance. Lowe’s Companies ended the day up 7.5%, but also had a midday spike to 15% before giving back some gains.

For comparison, the broad S&P 500 index ended the day up 1.6%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 3%, or more than 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since April 2025.

The stock market surge comes in the wake of Tuesday’s midterm election, where Democrats gained control of Congress in a dramatic sweep.

The homebuilding sector has faced massive cost increases in recent years. Several factors have played into the building sector’s hardships, which have led to a shortfall of roughly 4 million homes throughout the U.S., according to a March report from Realtor.com®.

Tariffs, supply chain issues, and inflation have caused substantial increases in material costs, according to Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial Group.

“Labor continues to be a major issue, with a shortage of skilled workers driving wages higher,” Gestiehr tells Realtor.com. “Add in land prices, permitting, insurance, and financing costs, and it becomes increasingly difficult to build homes at prices the average buyer can afford.”

Builders have experienced a squeeze from both sides, Gestiehr explains, because at the same time that the cost to build a home has increased, skyrocketing mortgage rates have put limits on what buyers can afford.

Just days ago, major builders including D.R. Horton and the PulteGroup reported net income declines, with PulteGroup CEO Ryan Marshall stating that the company’s year-over-year net income dropped by 17% in the third quarter.

Suddenly, there’s a renewed sense of optimism surrounding the industry after Tuesday’s election results.

While the underlying challenges remain, Gestiehr says that investors are likely expecting more federal attention to turn to policies surrounding affordability.

“Housing affordability has become a major concern, and investors may be anticipating more attention on policies that encourage new construction and make homeownership more affordable,” says Gestiehr. “Investors may be anticipating additional housing incentives, policies that encourage new construction, and potentially lower mortgage rates.”

Affordability, particularly when it comes to housing, was a key part of many Democratic candidate platforms.

To address affordability overall, there should be focus on building up the supply of homes before offering incentives for buyers and spurring more demand, says Gestiehr.

"If you increase demand without increasing supply, you may end up pushing home prices even higher,” adds Gestiehr. “Reducing regulatory costs, streamlining permitting, encouraging additional development, and potentially lowering tariffs on building materials could all help builders.”

Rolling back tariffs was a major talking point for several incoming Democrat senators, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Texas’ James Talarico, as well as Alaska’s Mary Peltola, whose race results were pending.

Gestiehr maintains that many other factors, including inflation, interest rates, employment, and corporate earnings, as well as actual policy changes, will still have a much greater impact on homebuilder results than the election results alone. It’s not uncommon for markets to perform well following midterm elections, in part because the uncertainty surrounding the election is removed.

“The election may have given homebuilders a reason to be optimistic, but optimism doesn't necessarily translate into stronger earnings,” says Gestiehr. “At some point, these companies need to see improvement in demand, affordability, and profit margins to justify higher stock prices.”

Congress already passed one major bipartisan housing bill this year, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. The bill lays out 45 provisions aimed at cutting red tape and constructing more homes, as well as banning institutional investor homebuyers.

Adding new members to Congress, many of whom have been elected on the promise of ushering in affordability, could mean more meaningful change is on the way.

“With a divided government, I wouldn’t expect major changes overnight, but housing affordability is an area where both parties have an incentive to find common ground,” says Gestiehr.

#5706. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5704. Why More Buyers Are Turning To Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Today

When mortgage rates climb, buying a home can start to feel like trying to hit a moving target. Every jump in rates makes monthly payments bigger, and that pushes a lot of buyers to look for another way in.

More and more of them are finding it in the adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM.

Here’s how an ARM differs from a more traditional mortgage. With a regular fixed-rate mortgage, your rate stays the same for your whole loan. But with an ARM, your rate is locked for the first few years, then it can move up or down based on market conditions.

Some people don’t like that level of uncertainty – and that’s okay. But others are drawn to this option specifically because there’s usually a lower rate to start when you opt for an ARM. And in an affordability-strapped market, that’s going to gain popularity.

Bankrate recently found that, in September, rates for ARM products were over a full percentage point lower than a regular fixed-rate loan. Depending on the ARM product, that can make a difference of $150-300 in the monthly payment on a median-priced home.

And for some buyers, that’s enough to turn “not right now” into “let’s do this.” You can see it in the numbers. Data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) shows that, in October, roughly 1 in 10 people applying for a mortgage chose an ARM (see graph below):

If you think you may want to consider this yourself, here’s what you need to know about how it works.

An ARM is like a phone or cable plan that has an introductory deal for new customers. You start out at a lower price, and then it adjusts after a specified amount of time. A popular loan is the 5/1 ARM.

The “5” means your introductory rate is locked for the first five years, and the “1” means that the rate can change every year after that. The rate change is called the “reset.” And here’s the really important part.

When your rate resets, your mortgage payment could go up or down. The good news is that most ARMs have caps, which are limits on how much your rate can rise each year and over the life of the loan. But either way, you have to be ready.

To see if this type of loan may be right for you, here are some things to think about and discuss with your loan officer:

Before you decide, ask your lender to work up the numbers and walk you through the different potential scenarios you could run into with an ARM. That way, you go in with your eyes open.

And, if you do go with an adjustable-rate mortgage, just know that you’ll have choices when the reset time arrives. You could:

Do nothing and keep your loan in place if the new payment still fits your budget.

Refinance into a fixed-rate loan with a payment that never changes.

Refinance into another ARM with a new lower rate locked for a specified timeframe.

Talk to the loan servicer about assistance or modification.

Remember, a refinance is a brand-new loan that you’ll have to qualify for – even if it’s on a home you already own. So, keep tabs on your credit and debt levels and ask your loan officer how major financial moves like job changes and major purchases will affect your mortgage readiness. It’s important to keep your credit and finances in “mortgage shape.”

One more quick note. ARMs got a bad name after the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, there were some risky loans with small starting payments that later shot way up. Others let people borrow without proving how much money they earned.

But now, there are new laws to protect both borrowers and lenders. The biggest change is the Ability-to-Repay Rule, which says that before a lender makes a home loan, it has to check real paperwork (like pay stubs, W-2 forms, and tax returns) to make sure you can afford it. The lender also has to look at what your payment could be after the reset, not just the low starting payment.

So, you don’t have to worry that today’s ARMs are the same as the ones we saw back during the crash.

Today's market has more options than many people realize. Finding the right one could be as simple as getting more information about tools like ARMs. A trusted lender can run the numbers with you, walk you through the what-ifs, and help you explore the possibilities.Is an ARM a good option for you? Talk to a loan officer to find out.

I took a lot of liberties in this apartment that I would not do in my family home or in my Greensboro home where I felt like it has to be more grown-up or something like that. I [felt] the freedom to be like, “That's the cutest thing I've ever seen. I'm gonna get that, whether it fits or not.”

I have a lot of my own creations in here, things that I've drawn or done. Honestly, the thing I'm most proud of in this apartment is my little basketball gold net chain that I constructed. Just yesterday I found these glasses [for] $8. They’re like wrought iron. I reorganized ... to make room for the glasses. I'm still constantly picking and refining and moving things, and I'm just such a person that needs to feel so good in my physical space.

In terms of the art and the shelving, I put a lot of work into making it fit me and my needs perfectly. I'm so particular and I like things done perfectly, measured perfectly, spaced perfectly.

I have ADHD, so I need little systems exactly how I need them to help me. If there's an extra step, then it's not going to happen.

I have a Russian handyman named Pavel. He is my lifesaver. Pavel and I have spent many, many hours together figuring out just how to make everything exactly how I wanted it, conducive to how I needed things. So no real renovations, but a lot of modifications.

I like to read here. I can see straight out the window at night. The skyline and the view is so beautiful and soothing. I see the moon. I see Venus right outside my window. It gives me a peace that I usually experience in nature. I love this little corner where I look out the window, or I can watch TV, or do whatever. I spend a lot of my time out here just sitting.

I actually spend a lot of time in the apartment because I don't have a 9-to-5 job that brings me out of the apartment. That is one of the biggest reasons I've put so much into it and wanted to feel so comfortable in it, because I'm here all the time.

I feel like I can be in the safety and comfort of my home and still feel like I'm in the world, which is something that I would never have in Greensboro. That's something that I really missed. I really do feel like this specific apartment is such a big part of my experience in Charlotte. I'm very attached to it.

#5702. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. #5701. Real REMAX Q3 Revenue Skyrockets; Company ‘Offboards’ Over 1,000 Agents

After the Real Brokerage completed its acquisition of RE/MAX Holdings this past August, the third quarter earnings for the company revealed a significant shift in revenue, sparked by AI investments and slight drops in agent retention.

Tamir Poleg—Real REMAX chairman and CEO—started off the first earnings call for the combined companies, and expressed his confidence in “delivering strong growth in adjusted EBITDA” even if the housing market “gets worse.”

He also acknowledged the increases in agent offboarding. The Q3 earnings release stated that 500 agents had been let go in October alone, with the total REMAX agent count in the U.S. and Canada reportedly down 3% from the previous year at 72,118.

“The housing market has been operating near trough levels for the past four years,” Poleg added. “The recent increase in mortgage rates has further delayed the recovery that many, myself included, had anticipated. Beginning in September, we saw an uptick in the number of agents leaving the industry altogether. Real REMAX Group was not immune. Over the past two months, we’ve proactively offboarded more than 1,000 agents, many of whom allowed their real estate licenses to expire or left the industry.”

Real REMAX Group President Jenna Rozenblat echoed Poleg’s sentiment and noted that personnel other than agents were let go throughout the third quarter.

“We’ve reduced our combined headcount by more than 14%, which translates to over 150 positions across the organization while simplifying management structures and consolidating overlapping functions,” she stated.

While the series of layoffs and offboarding can be a cause for concern for some agents, Rozenblat emphasized the reason why restructuring is taking place, and mentioned the importance of AI technology.

“We don’t expect an immediate reversal in agent attrition in a franchise business, but our priority is to improve franchise owner economics and help them deliver a more competitive value proposition to agents and the clients they serve,” she continued. “Technology is an important part of that effort. We have already begun alpha testing Real’s proprietary reason software and AI capabilities for a phase rollout to the broader REMAX network.”

Poleg also briefly addressed a question on Open Real Estate, the initiative promising a new platform for listing distribution.

Poleg said Real REMAX believed strongly in its principles of “a more open, transparent and competitive approach to how real estate data is distributed,” but declined to comment on “specific products, economics or revenue opportunities” stemming from Open Real Estate.

On the point of AI, October’s introduction of Leo Pro—Real REMAX’s AI platform for agents and brokerages—could have instigated the large offboarding process. Poleg pointed out how Leo Pro can perform the functions “that traditionally required hiring additional staff, paying for multiple software subscriptions or spending hundreds of hours doing the work yourself.”

“The main usage of Leo Pro we’re seeing is creating marketing materials, social media posts and working their CRMs. It’s mostly nurturing their leads, and we’re seeing great conversions for our agents in terms of scheduling appointments for them and listing agreements,” Poleg stated.

Poleg also claimed that “historically, there has been a lot of disappointment with what REMAX has been offering their agents and brokers” in terms of tech, and that he has seen a lot of excitement from franchise owners.

“The fact that we have mature technology that is serving the Real side on the brokerage side gives them a lot of confidence that this is proven technology that can help them run better businesses,” Poleg said.

The data for the Q3 earnings call predates the release of Leo Pro.

Overall, the Real REMAX Group’s revenue increased 28% on a yearly basis, clocking in at nearly $728 million for Q3. The Q3 revenue for 2025 was $568.5 million.

The jump in revenue can mostly be attributed to the acquisition, as the release also notes that assuming the acquisition had taken place on Jan. 1, 2025 (a pro forma basis). It’s estimated that the combined revenue had increased by 20% instead to $770 million, compared to the prior year’s $641.8 million.

“On a pro forma basis, combined revenue increased 20% year-over-year to approximately $770 million compared with a 2% decline in industry existing-home sales transactions in the quarter,” Real REMAX CFO Ravi Jani said. “Within our brokerage business, Real continued to gain market share, while our franchise business continues to see attrition in North America.”

As for profitability, the company’s operating loss clocked in at $72 million for the third quarter, a significant increase from last year’s loss of $0.5 million. Jani attributed the growth in operating loss to the $52.3 million in acquisition-related expenses, and another $26.4 million in accelerated stock-based compensation related to employee terminations following the acquisition.

Net loss also grew dramatically year-over-year, at $67.2 million—or $2.25 per diluted share—for Q3. Last year’s Q3 net losses were estimated to be $0.3 million, or only $0.02 per diluted share.

Despite significant growth in losses and expenses—primarily caused by the acquisition—Real REMAX’s adjusted EBITDA increased 66% to $33.8 million in Q3, compared to $20.4 million the same period last year. The adjusted EBITDA margin also increased slightly by 4.6%, whereas last year’s margin was 3.6%.

For the final quarter of 2026, Jani expects revenue to fall, while EBITDA maintains itself in the mid-$30 million range.

“For the fourth quarter of 2026, we’re expecting continued pressure on housing activity, including declines in transactions per agent at Real and a year-over-year decline in REMAX’s North American agent count,” he concluded. “Against that backdrop, we expect fourth quarter revenue of $575 million to $625 million and adjusted EBITDA of $32 million to $38 million.”

Leo Pro may take center stage in the company’s Q4 earnings call and throughout 2027, as Poleg mentioned that plans to roll out the AI platform for the entire REMAX network are underway.

“Within a few weeks, we want to roll out Leo Pro for the entire REMAX network. Our operating platform for the broker/owners will be ready at some point in Q1 2027,” Poleg added. “I think that once that’s in place, we will be able to help a lot of the broker/owners with some of their struggles around profitability, freeing up time to focus on agent attraction and teaching their agents on how to sell more.”

#5700. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

#5699. Generational Wealth Fuels Record-High Levels of Cash Sales Among First-Time Buyers

The share of first-time homebuyers paying all cash has climbed to record levels, fueled by generational wealth transfers, even as eroding affordability continues to push homeownership out of reach for many Americans.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, 10% of rookie home shoppers paid all cash instead of relying on financing, marking the largest percentage on record, according to the annual Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers released Thursday by the National Association of Realtors®.

The data also reveals that all-cash buyers were roughly three times likelier than financed first-time buyers to have used an inheritance (28% vs. 9%).

Across all first-time buyers—cash or financed—10% used an inheritance toward their home purchase, marking a new record and the fourth straight annual increase.

"The housing market is beginning to see a generational transfer of wealth. It’s not yet a tsunami, but it is changing who can buy a first home and when," says Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research. "Because people are living longer, the generation receiving that wealth isno longer young adults. Many are reaching middle age before they can buy their first home."

In fact, while the median age of first-time buyers held steady at a record high of 40, cash buyers skewed older, with the median age reaching 54 years old, compared to 38 for those who used financing.

Echoing Lautz, Realtor.com® senior economist Hannah Jones confirms that the transfer of wealth from one generation to the next is starting to show up in the housing market, though the full effect won't likely be felt for a few more years.

Older homeowners hold substantial equity, and repeat buyers, with a median age of 62—matching a record high set last year— paid all cash 30% of the time in 2026. Jones says that for some rookie buyers, that wealth arrives as an inheritance.

"Buyers with access to inherited wealth have a significant advantage when they can purchase without financing," Anthony Mian, an agent with Douglas Elliman Beverly Hills, tells Realtor.com. "In multiple-offer situations, sellers often favor all-cash offers because they eliminate financing risk, reduce the likelihood of delays, and provide greater certainty of closing."

Other avenues open to baby boomers wishing to boost their children's or grandchildren's purchasing power include cash gifted toward a down payment, co-signing a loan, or selling investment properties, says Emilee Warner, a real estate agent at MW Real Estate Co. in Nashville, TN.

Looking at the top sources for a down payment among first-time buyers, personal savings continued to dominate (62%), followed by financial assets, such as 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency (30%), and gifts or loans from family and friends (25%).

"Wealth, whether built up or inherited, is increasingly what gets some buyers in, while buyers who depend on a mortgage still face high rates and prices," notes Jones.

Warner says she recently worked with first-time buyers who paid all cash borrowed the "bank" of mom and dad to purchase a home with a price tag exceeding $1 million.

"The cash buyers out there want to get in a home prior to rates dropping," Warner tells Realtor.com. "They are serious, willing, and able buyers. Cash allows appraisals to be waived, removing the risk of a low appraisal that could lose a financed buyer the home."

While more than half of repeat buyers (57%) relied on proceeds from the sale of their previous home and 42% used savings for their down payment, harnessing generational wealth among this cohort is not unheard of, with 4% using an inheritance or a gift from a family member or friend to fund their next home purchase.

Brandon Winn, an agent at Iowa Realty in Des Moines, IA, says he recently worked with move-up buyers who were purchasing a home with the help of their parents who offered them a 3% loan.

"This was when interest rates were 6.5%, and they gave them a 3% loan so they could afford to buy the home that they wanted," Winn tells Realtor.com.

Winn adds that at the luxury tier of the Des Moines market topping $600,000, he is seeing a growing number of buyers paying all cash using either inheritance or investment funds.

"Interest rates have risen so quickly that it's priced a lot of buyers out of the market," says the agent. "So if you have the cash ... it gives you the opportunity to purchase the house without having a [mortgage] payment, and then, of course, you're going to build equity quite a bit faster."

Mian, in Beverly Hills, says that for young families, that additional disposable income can go toward childcare, education, savings, or investments. Access to generational wealth can even expand their housing search geographically.

"In a market as expensive as Los Angeles, this can influence not only who can afford to purchase a home, but also which neighborhoods they can access and how much financial flexibility they retain after purchasing," he says. "Ultimately, generational wealth is becoming an important factor in determining both housing opportunities and long-term financial security."

Affordability continues to be the biggest major hurdle for aspiring U.S. homeowners.

The share of first-time buyers ticked up to 22% from last year's all-time low of 21%, yet it is still roughly half the historical norm of 40% recorded before 2008. Jones attributes the modest year-over-year boost to mortgage rate declines in the beginning of 2026.

Rates briefly dipped below 6% in February, before the outbreak of the Iran war, and were below year-ago levels from October 2025 through July 2026.

"This presented a window of opportunity for first-time buyers relying on a mortgage. The vast majority of first-time buyers financed their purchase, which means the median first-time buyer age is closer to the financed first-time buyer age," says Jones. "All-cash first-time buyers have aged 10 years in a decade, versus six for financed buyers, which shows they are a different group, middle-aged and drawing on savings, investments or inheritance."

Examining the makeup of first-time buyers in 2026, NAR data shows the share of first-time buyers who were married couples decreased slightly to 47%. Single women accounted for a quarter of all first-time buyers, same as in 2025, while the share of single men climbed to 12%, the highest level since 2011.

The typical novice buyer in 2026 had a median household income of $100,000, up from last year's $94,400.

The median down payment among first-time buyers this year was 9%, down from 10% in 2025 and significantly below the 18% recorded among all buyers.

As in years past, equity-rich repeat buyers continued to dominate the market, accounting for 78% of all home purchases with a median household income of $127,000 and a typical down payment of 19%— more than double that of first-timers. Nearly a third (30%) paid all cash.

"Repeat buyers are driving the housing market," says Lautz. "Unlike first-time home buyers, repeat buyers have seen their housing equity grow rapidly over the past decade, enabling them to trade up for larger homes or move into more desirable locations. These are often moves by choice rather than necessity."

The typical home seller in 2026 has owned their property for 12 years, a new all-time high surpassing last year's 11-year tenure. Forty-seven percent of sellers went on to purchase a newer home, and 36% bought a larger home.

Of all homes sold on the market, 78% did not have children under the age of 18 residing in the home, down from 81% last year.

For all sellers, the most commonly cited reason for selling their home was the desire to move closer to friends and family (22%), followed by the home being too small (12%), the home being too large (10%), a change in family situation (8%), and moving due to retirement (8%).

For recently sold homes, the final sales price was a median of 99% of the final listing price.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

"It's about enjoying it as much as possible. This will be my last World Cup, but let's hope tomorrow isn't my last game," the star athlete said, according to ESPN.

"I don't need it, I have a good life, but it's about passion. I play football because I love it. ... You have to enjoy every day. And I've scored three goals [at this World Cup], I'm not doing too badly, right?" Ronaldo said.

#5697. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5696. Data Centers Meet Fierce Backlash From Voters as Dozens of Towns Reject New Projects

Data centers appeared on the ballot in 41 communities across 12 states this week, and in nearly every case, voters resoundingly voted to restrict or ban them, a sign that backlash continues to grow against the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence.

Of the 41 ballot initiatives, only Harwood, ND, passed a pro-data center ordinance. Voters there rejected a ballot initiative that would have required the city to create an independent review paid for by the developer to evaluate the impact of data centers in the community.

In Ohio, which has seemingly become an epicenter of the data center debate, 18 counties put data centers on the ballot. Many measures did not outright ban data centers, but set limits on noise pollution, water and energy use, and other environmental concerns.

Tech companies have poured millions into expanding Ohio's already substantial number of data centers. AI and crypto political action committees spent an estimated $65 million to influence the Ohio midterms, backing Republican Senator John Husted, who lost re-election to Democrat Sherrod Brown on Tuesday.

Both Hubbard, OH and Urbana, OH, passed outright bans on data centers, while other communities passed initiatives that would greatly limit or restrict data center growth based on size and energy usage.

Hubbard resident Jenny Goldberg organized against the data centers in her community.

“We now have the power to say no,” she told WFMJ. “Let's put the brakes on. Let's wait to see if you know if environmental changes, if technology changes, make something like this possible in the future. Then we can reconsider it.”

In Ashville, OH, more than 80% of voters supported a measure intended to overturn a municipal agreement allowing developer EdgeConneX to construct a pair of facilities locally. The ballot measure will not halt construction on the projects, but proponents hope it will send a message to the state’s power board to reject EdgeConneX’s request for a power plant.

Elsewhere in the state, voters rejected measures intended to rezone land for data center use.

Next November, Ohio voters will weigh in on the Ohio Prohibition of Data Center Construction Amendment, which would prohibit data centers that exceed 25 megawatts of monthly demand across the state.

Similar outright bans passed in North Berwick, ME; Americus, KS; Alhambra, CA; Edgewater, FL; and Canterbury, NH.

In Maine, eight counties voted to support initiatives that would ban or place moratoriums on data center construction, and in Illinois, seven ballot measures restricting data centers passed.

Proponents of data centers tout them as economic boons for communities, but the Brookings Institution says that boon is often overstated.

Brookings studied the impact of data centers on employment and found that certain sectors do benefit, though the economic impact is often overstated.

Wages tend to remain stagnant compared with the impact of data centers on housing prices, which have historically received a bump of between 2% and 5% where data centers are built.
