#5653. Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep

Shares of Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc. closed higher today following Democrats’ resounding midterm victory.

Amazon jumped 8.3% at one point and ended the trading session 6.1% higher than Tuesday. Microsoft gained nearly 6.7% while Alphabet and Google rose by about 3.1% and 1.4%, respectively. Multiple industry analysts tied the stock gains to the companies’ artificial intelligence buildout.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress on a campaign that emphasized data center restrictions. Furthermore, voters approved 40 ballot measures focused on blocking or limiting AI infrastructure projects. Bloomberg cited Robert Pavlik, a senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, as saying that tech giants’ shares jumped because investors believe a data center slowdown could improve their finances.

Amazon, Meta and Google have become cash-flow-negative in recent months because of their steep infrastructure investments. Last Wednesday, the search giant reported a negative cash flow that exceeded the consensus estimate by about $6.4 billion. Google’s stock price plummeted 10% in after-hours trading even though its cloud revenue more than doubled.

Needham & Co., B. ‌Riley ⁠Wealth and prominent tech industry analyst Ben Thompson highlighted another possible contributor to the stock rally. New restrictions on AI projects would make computing infrastructure more scarce, which would boost the value of existing data centers. That would benefit the tech giants that logged share price gains today.

Thompson noted that neoclouds, or emerging AI-focused cloud providers, may also benefit in certain respects. Developments for which they have already secured regulatory permission could become more valuable. At the same time, they may find it more difficult to finance new sites.

That dynamic weighed on chip stocks today. Nvidia Corp. and Intel Corp. both shed more than 3% of their value, while Broadcom Inc. declined 2%. SK hynix Inc., the world’s largest supplier of HBM memory for graphics cards, dropped by more than 5%. One notable exception was Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which ended the trading day about 1% higher.

Thompson noted that the midterms could also affect the AI industry in other ways. He pointed out that a stricter regulatory environment may give space-based data centers a boost. Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, in turn, could see their hardware costs decline if new restrictions are placed on frontier model training. Such a development may ease their path to profitability.

Last month, Meta announced plans to sell up to $95 billion in shares to finance new data centers. On Monday, Oracle Corp. filed to issue $20 billion worth of bonds and shares in connection with its own AI buildout. It’s currently unclear how the midterm results will affect those initiatives and other large-scale data center projects currently underway.

#5652. EXCLUSIVE: Ryan Serhant Warns Homebuyers Against Waiting for 2027: ‘You Don’t Want to Wait Until It’s Too Late’

Ryan Serhant is warning would-be homebuyers against assuming that lower mortgage rates will deliver an easier path to homeownership in 2027—and says the housing market has a problem that cheaper borrowing alone cannot solve.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, Serhant shared his outlook for the year ahead, identified markets he believes could surprise buyers, and weighed in on the debate over private listings.

He also offered a glimpse inside his own townhouse and revealed a buyer request that has him searching for an enormous stretch of land with its own airport.

At the center of his housing outlook is a concern about people at opposite ends of the property ladder being unable to move.

“We have entered an environment where people can't afford to buy their first home, and their parents can't afford to leave their last one, and it's a problem we need to solve," he said.

“Lower mortgage rates will help, but rates alone are not going to fix the cost of housing or the cost of moving. We need to create more supply and fewer obstacles," Serhant added.

Serhant argued that the system has become an obstacle to moving, with consequences that have developed over many years.

“I think that what we've created is a environment, that is punishing mobility. Instead of rewarding mobility. And this was set up a long, long time ago. We didn't get here overnight.”

“Like, the housing market and the system we operate in rewards stability, because what's… it makes everyone feel comfortable. But then when that stability does not move, because stability is stability, mobility is mobility. Then everyone gets angry, and that's the environment that we're currently in.”

For his outlook, he is watching whether households have both the confidence and the resources to act.

“I think I'm watching employment, and I'm watching household confidence right now. I think pent-up demand only becomes a transaction when people have the confidence and the financial ability to act, and we'll see if that happens anytime soon.”

For people who can afford to buy but are considering waiting for a better deal in 2027, Serhant pointed to opportunities he believes already exist.

“I think in a lot of markets, we've entered a buyer's market now. You have the ability to negotiate in markets that you haven't been able to negotiate in in the past couple years.”

“I think there's a great opportunity to use the rate pressure that we have to negotiate closing costs, to negotiate rate buy-downs, to negotiate lower purchase prices, to get a house that really, really, really works for you. Remember, it is such an old and annoying saying, but you do marry the house, and you do date through the rates.”

His argument rests on the potential trade-off between borrowing costs and competition, although his comments about future rates and inventory are predictions.

“The market does become very stagnant. Interest rates should come down, and remember, you can refinance. And you should use the opportunity right now, if you can afford it, to purchase in a high-interest rate environment, because there's less competition.”

“Everyone wants low rates, they never want what comes with it. You know what'll happen if rates come down? There will be no houses for sale.”

“You won't even have the opportunity to complain about a high monthly payment. You won't even be able to talk about—the lack of affordability. You won't be able to complain, because there will be nothing for sale, because the demand is so great. There is not nearly enough houses for the demand we have in this country. Every 40-year-old who still lives at home will then move.”

Serhant also argued that the circumstances accompanying lower rates can make buyers reluctant to purchase.

“And what also brings down low interest rates is job insecurity. You know, is unemployment, is war. Are things that happen in the global environment that will make people, not confident to go and make a massive purchase. And so, you might miss that opportunity, too.”

He used the early months of the pandemic to illustrate his point about confidence and timing.

“In the spring of 2020, that was a great time to buy. But no, we had COVID, 'You can't buy. There's a death ticker on the bottom of every TV screen. You might not live.' You didn't take advantage of this environment, and then when the market came back, it was too late.”

“And so, I would use this moment to move quickly, because when things do even out, and they always do, markets go up and markets go down. Always. And forever. You don't want to wait until it's too late.”

Serhant highlighted returning city residents and investment in jobs as themes behind his market picks.

“I think people are returning to cities in a way that we haven't seen before. It's one of the reasons we just were launching, officially Chicago. This coming Wednesday. I'm incredibly excited about that.”

“The demand and the volume we've seen from all of our other Serhant markets wanting to move back to Chicago, who moved out over the past couple years. Taking advantage of good value, like we just talked about, is really exciting.”

“And I think places where you're seeing incredible job growth. Areas like Ohio, where there's major, major tech investment, not just in data centers. In office. And in manufacturing.”

“We have a lot of investment that's going into Western Pennsylvania, and, you're also seeing a lot of movement into Alabama.”

“You know, I think there are markets that will really, really surprise you because of great quality of life for the best cost structure the country has to offer.”

Serhant also addressed private listings, beginning with his explanation of how they differ from properties marketed publicly.

“A private listing is the opposite of a public to the consumer listing," he said.

“It has been the standard over the past… 20-some-odd years—that if you want to market your home, so that there is a fair and free market and competitive marketplace, that if you opt to work with a real estate agent. That you have to bring your home to the public marketplace.”

“Obviously, every home that's not on the market is technically a private listing. The Empire State Building is a private listing, for what it's worth. The whole world is a private listing.”

He then offered his criticism of listing restrictions and penalties. The following is his characterization of the debate, rather than a description of a single policy applying to every platform or multiple listing service.

“But what has changed now is the MLSs, and the listing aggregators have installed fees and penalties.”

“So, if you list with them, as you're supposed to, you can have the prize of being public, but if you don't list with them, because you want to work with an agent, but you don't want your home to be blasted all over the world, then you can never list with them ever, and we will also punish you, potentially with fines.”

“The current debate is over, should that be allowed? Who actually owns the data, and who actually owns the property? And access to it. Is it the brokerage? Is it the websites that showcase listings? Is it the multiple listing services? Is it the owner of the property?”

For Serhant, the discussion should focus on what sellers receive from the process.

“And that's what the debate is over right now, is what they say, consumer choice. I think what is broken is that it's not about consumer choice. I think everyone's focused on the wrong thing. I think people should be focused on consumer value.”

“Where's the upside? Where's the consumer upside? You know, the battle right now is over commission fees, and who gets a piece. And I think that's gross, and I'm in this business.”

On concerns that private listings could reduce a seller's pool of buyers or disadvantage people without the right connections, Serhant acknowledged the risks.

“I think there are real concerns. But I think everybody has to be fully aware of what those concerns are. And again, I think it should be up to the consumer, and unfortunately, these rules exist because in a world where there is no rules, and there is no punishment. Not everyone is a good actor.”

He drew on his own experience working as an agent during the financial crisis.

“Like, all the people that are leading this fight, none of them were real estate agents like I was in 2008 and 2009. None of them were trying to get business on Craigslist. None of them were trying to figure out what was for sale and what wasn't for sale.”

“None of them were trying to figure out if the listing agent in front of them was lying to their client or not. None of them were trying to figure out, with the fiduciary responsibility of a buyer in front of you, how to give them the most accurate and up-to-date information.”

“None of them were, like me, on the streets of New York City, or trying to do deals in Florida and California, trying to figure out what is actually for sale, and if a buyer isn't paying an excise commission by working with that agent, they actually won't even get that property? Is that really? What we want to go back to?”

“I feel like a homeowner's value and a homeowner's biggest asset shouldn't become a real estate brokerage's, or an MLS's, or a listing aggregator's recruiting tool.”

Away from the business of buying and selling, Serhant shared the first thing he does when he walks into his townhouse.

“I yell out my daughter's name. I wanted to see where she is in my house. We have a townhouse, so I'm trying to figure out which floor she's on, so I can, you know, prepare.”

His favorite spaces include a gym on the lower level, although his affection extends to the whole property.

“I have a pretty awesome gym. In the lower level that I built out, that's really, really cool, and I think that's pretty awesome, but I mean, I built it with my bare hand. It was a TV show that we did for Bravo about our renovation, and I love that house. Whole thing is great.”

He also described the practical details that help make his kitchen work, starting with a concealed ladder for reaching high cabinets.

“We have incredibly high ceilings. So we have a hidden ladder in our kitchen that looks like the baseboard under the kitchen. Island, and it pops out with the touch of your toe.”

“And, the ladder shows up, and so for anyone, you know, you know, who's vertically challenged to be able to reach upper cabinetry without having a ladder in front of your face at all times, so that you can still enjoy all that light and sunshine and high ceilings, I think is key.”

“Probably the greatest things that we have also in that kitchen are touchless, so, like, the sink, you know, you're cooking, and your hands are messy, and you're always hitting the thing. We have the kitchen sink, where all you have to do is tap it, and it turns on.”

“And so you just hit it with the back of your hand, and it turns on. So you're not, like, also getting the sink and the faucet dirty.”

“And then the same thing for the kitchen refrigerator and freezer. All you do is you slowly kind of, like, tap it with your elbow, or with the side, so you're not, like, yanking on anything, and it automatically just reveals itself to you. I think those little touches are overlooked.”

Among the unusual requests Serhant receives, one current search involves a vast amount of land—and a private airport.

“They're all wild. I'm dealing with somebody right now that wants 100,000 acres of land, which is impossible, for the most part."

For all the features a buyer might want, Serhant has one clear priority when choosing a home.

“You can change everything about the house you want over the years, you can grow into it, you can grow out of it, you can update it, you can paint it, you can flip it upside down. Unless you are Ken Griffin, and you can pick up a house, and you can move it, for the most part. Change the location.”

“And so, you always buy location first. Whatever that is, wherever that place is you want to be for the next 5-10 years, and most times you're paying more. But no one ever paid too much. And regretted it years later. Very, very rarely does that happen.”

“Remember, if you buy a trophy, you get to sell a trophy. If you buy a discount, because you're cheap, you will have to sell a discount. And you will feel cheap.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. #5651. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5650. The chips are down: Qualcomm falls on revenue miss, weak guidance; Arm and GlobalFoundries do little better

Chipmakers Qualcomm Inc., Arm Holdings Ltd. and GlobalFoundries Ltd. struggled to move the needle today after reporting financial results that clearly left investors wanting more.

After an impressive earnings beat from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. just 24 hours earlier, investors may have had heightened expectations. But if they did, on a day when the market rocketed higher on the U.S. election results, they were clearly let down by the shaky performance of Qualcomm, which beat expectations on earnings but missed on revenue and offered weak guidance. The result was predictable, with its stock down more than 6% after-hours.

Both Arm and GlobalFoundries did better, but it wasn’t enough to satisfy investors who are becoming increasingly concerned about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence industry that has driven significant growth for all three chipmakers over the last couple of years.

The biggest disappointment was Qualcomm, which reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.17 per share on revenue of $10.44 billion, up just 8% from a year earlier. The results were mixed, with Wall Street looking for earnings of $2.16 per share on sales of $10.48 billion. For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it’s looking for earnings of around $2.25 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range on sales of $10.48 billion, falling short of the Street’s target of $2.27 per share in earnings and $10.48 billion in revenue.

Qualcomm’s troubles stem from the fact that it has less exposure to the AI industry’s rampant growth than many other chipmakers. The bulk of its sales comes from system-on-chips and modems for smartphones. But the market is currently reeling due to the rising cost of components such as memory, which have forced handset makers to bump up their prices, reducing demand. Qualcomm has tried to weather the storm by raising the prices of its own chips recently, but its smartphone chip sales fell 26% in the quarter to just $5.14 billion, well behind the Street’s target of $5.21 billion.

Under Chief Executive Cristiano Amon (pictured), Qualcomm has tried to pivot and grow its position in alternative chip markets, particularly the AI data center industry. Revenue from that segment rose to $650 million during the quarter, but it’s still dwarfed by the smartphone business.

Nonetheless, Amon insisted that the company will grow its data center business to more than $5 billion in revenue by the end of fiscal 2027. He said the company recently struck a deal with an unnamed global hyperscaler for optical connectivity chips. “We don’t have a demand issue; it’s a supply issue,” he told analysts on a conference call. “If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better.”

Qualcomm’s automotive business was a bright spot, with sales there rising 89% to $1.99 billion in the quarter, above the Street’s consensus estimate of $1.66 billion. Internet of Things revenue came to $1.88 billion, up 4% from a year ago and just ahead of the Street’s estimate.

Finally, there’s Qualcomm’s QTL business, which generates revenue from licensing intellectual property for modems, 5G connectivity and other technologies. That segment added $1.3 billion in revenue, down 7%, despite signing renewed licensing agreements with Apple Inc., Transsion Inc. and Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd.

Chip design company Arm delivered much more palatable results, but it was somewhat cautious with its guidance for the current quarter, and its stock was down 2% in late trading today. The company reported adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, just beating the Street’s target of 48 cents, while revenue rose 27% from a year earlier, to $1.44 billion, ahead of the $1.38 billion analyst estimate.

Unlike Qualcomm, Arm doesn’t manufacture complete chips for its customers, but instead designs and licenses processor blueprints for customers such as Apple Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Qualcomm to build their own custom chips. Where Arm is more similar to Qualcomm is in its strategy, where it too is also pivoting to focus on data center chip designs, trying to tap into the demand for AI compute. Arm said its data center business was the main growth driver this year, with royalties there doubling year-over-year.

However, Arm’s guidance did little to excite investors. The company said it’s looking for earnings of 56 cents per share, plus or minus four cents, compared with Wall Street’s forecast of 55 cents per share. For revenue, it’s targeting $1.54 billion, plus or minus $50 million, which is just ahead of the Street’s $1.52 billion target.

GlobalFoundries did a little better than its peers today, posting results and guidance for the current that squeaked past expectations. However, its stock remained flat after-hours.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on sales of $1.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, with growth driven by strong demand from AI and data center customers, it said. The results were better than expected, with analysts targeting earnings of 51 cents on revenue of $1.89 billion.

GlobalFoundries’ also differs from Qualcomm, in that it’s a pure-play contract manufacturer that builds the processors designed by semiconductors firms, rather than designing chips itself or selling them under its own brand. Qualcomm is actually one of its biggest customers, alongside Broadcom Inc., NXP Semiconductors N.V. and Infineon Technologies Inc. As such, its fortunes are very much aligned with those of the chip designers it caters too.

For the current quarter, GlobalFoundries said it’s looking for earnings of 59 cents per share, plus or minus five cents, on revenue of about $2 billion. Wall Street is looking for earnings of 57 cents per share and has the same revenue target.

#5649. French blood banks hacked amid ‘deeply concerning’ wave of fridge and freezer cyberattacks in Europe

In a recent spate of cyberattacks in Europe against fridges and freezers, the latest assault hit France’s national blood service, where hackers gained control of cold storage systems at medical facilities and turned up the temperature.

The French Blood Establishment, EFS, told media that the facilities managed to save the blood supplies and there has been “no loss of blood products.” But the attacks come after supermarkets in several European countries experienced hacks of their fridges and freezers leading to the loss of millions of Euros in products.

Last month, hackers hit hundreds of supermarkets across France where temperatures were forced up to 50 degrees C overnight in what officials called an “unprecedented” attack. Food losses and fires were reported after “connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France.” What followed was a wave of similar attacks across the continent where fridges and freezers at stores in the U.K., Italy and Germany were recently hacked, following attacks in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine ​consumers’ confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously,” said EU Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.”

Connected fridges can now be controlled and monitored remotely through internet-connected software but with this comes vulnerabilities. Hackers can exploit publicly reachable, legacy or unpatched remote refrigeration management controllers that may use default passwords or weak date-based administrative bypasses.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, told Reuters.

Cybersecurity experts so far have not figured out who’s behind the attacks. Russian hacking groups are a possibility as well as Iranian hacktivists or nation-state hackers. It might also be kids pulling off what have so far been very expensive pranks. Cybersecurity researchers at some firms have installed fake software as honeypots in an attempt to gather information about the hackers.

#5648. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5647. Bitcoin Bounces Back From 6-Week Low Despite $1B ETF Exodus

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin bounced back above $78,000 just now after hitting a six-week low, even as U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF sheds $1.16 billion across three trading sessions. The recovery came as daily withdrawals slowed sharply, giving BTC buyers room to push back after a steep selloff following the expected Democrats’ congressional win.

BTC climbed to $78,500, recovering from its overnight plunge as crypto markets rallied alongside U.S. stock futures. The rebound followed a difficult stretch for Bitcoin, with security concerns and political uncertainty weighing on investor sentiment.

The latest Bitcoin ETF figures show selling pressure easing, but institutional investors have yet to return in force. Withdrawals dropped from $643.2 million on October 30 to $115.6 million on November 3, while Bitcoin recovered from its six-week low.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF recorded three consecutive sessions of net withdrawals, totaling approximately $1.16 billion. The fund lost $643.2 million on October 30, followed by $398.6 million on November 2 and another $115.6 million on November 3.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) led Tuesday’s withdrawals with $95 million in outflows. Grayscale’s Bitcoin Mini Trust lost another $52.6 million, adding to the pressure on the funds.

Several products still attracted fresh capital. Bitwise’s BITB recorded $21.9 million in inflows, while Fidelity’s FBTC added $6.8 million. Morgan Stanley’s MSBT also attracted $3.3 million.

The latest Bitcoin ETF data shows daily withdrawals falling by more than 80% from Friday’s peak. October also ended with roughly $515 million in net outflows, while November’s first three reported sessions added another $1.16 billion in withdrawals.

The slowdown offers a more encouraging signal for Bitcoin bulls, although the funds remain firmly in net-outflow territory. Institutional investors are still reducing exposure rather than rebuilding positions.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin’s recovery comes after a sharp selloff that pushed it to its lowest level in six weeks. The market has faced several pressures simultaneously, including the recent Binance security breach and uncertainty surrounding U.S. crypto legislation.

Democrats winning control of both congressional chambers raised questions about the industry’s legislative agenda. However, Bitcoin recovered alongside stock markets just now as the initial reaction gave way to renewed buying.

$80,000 is now the focus, with the next resistance zone sitting between $79,500 and $80,000. A break above that range could open the door toward $82,000, particularly if ETF outflows continue shrinking. The sharp decline in daily withdrawals shows institutional selling is losing some momentum, giving BTC a chance to extend its recovery.

However, Bitcoin needs to reclaim $80,000 to turn the bounce into a stronger bullish move. Failure to clear that level could leave BTC vulnerable to another rejection, especially with ETF investors still pulling capital. A return below $77,000 would expose the recent $75,600 low, where buyers previously stepped in.

The immediate outlook hinges on whether Bitcoin can turn $78,000 into support and challenge $80,000 with stronger buying volume. Slowing ETF withdrawals offer an encouraging backdrop, but a sustained move higher would require renewed spot demand rather than another short-lived relief rally.

#5646. An 18th-Century Connecticut Estate With ‘Little Women’ Ties Lists for $1.5 Million—Hidden Treasures Included

An 18th-century antique home in Wolcott, CT, with ties to a famous clockmaker and the Trans-Siberian Orchestra just hit the market for $1.5 million.

Listed for the first time in decades, the 1.94-acre property known as Spindle Hill includes a 5,360-square-foot primary residence, a hand-hewn barn, a manor home, an a history of treasure-filled walls.

"When you walk into the original section of the home, you feel the history," says listing agent Donna Membrino of William Pitt Sotheby’s International Realty. "The keeping room has an original beehive oven and a wooden mantel."

The property’s origins date to the early 1700s, when the land was purchased by the town’s first settler, the patriarch of the Alcott family, according to Membrino. Nathaniel Lane and Millicent Alcott Lane, the uncle and aunt of "Little Women" author Louisa May Alcott, later developed it into a working farm that stayed in the Lane family for generations.

The property is also linked to famed clockmaker Seth Thomas, who launched his first clockmaking venture from his childhood home just down the road.

“It was very important to the seller to preserve the home’s history, and they have taken great pains to do that,” Membrino says.

Marlene Tosun, who grew up on Spindle Hill Farm, became the owner of the property in the 1950s.

After moving in, she uncovered a series of hidden treasures: a violin beneath the floorboards of the main house; Nathaniel Lane’s diary, containing his handwritten business accounts, tucked behind a wall; and tomahawk heads embedded in the estate’s original hand-stacked stone walls, which are believed to have been built by Native Americans.

Membrino said the family also discovered a pair of 1700s wheels from Lane’s ox-drawn wagon, which was used to deliver goods to early New England customers.

The seller, Marlene’s daughter Sylvia Tosun, was once the lead vocalist for the Trans-Siberian Orchestra. She also featured on an international EDM hit championed by DJ Armin van Buuren.

In a meticulous restoration, Tosun set out to preserve the property’s original charm and character while bringing it up to modern luxury standards.

Original weathered wood salvaged from older, dismantled sections of the house was used to detail the Grand Salon. Other highlights include a black-and-white marble foyer, a 50-foot turret with an antique Schonbek chandelier, double-height cathedral ceilings, reclaimed wide-plank heart pine floors, a handcarved Italian marble chimneypiece, and three wood-burning fireplaces.

A modernized kitchen with Shaker cabinetry and granite countertops flows into a sunny dining room. Upstairs, the primary suite has a private terrace. The walk-out garden level features a wet bar and a “grand fireplace lounge” that serves as a professional recording studio.

The property also offers twin gazebos, a sunken patio, fruit trees and vegetable gardens, as well as “rare legal multi-family zoning” that allows for three private dwellings.

“Wolcott is a great town,” Membrino adds. “It’s close to Waterbury and Hartford but has more of a country feel, and it’s centrally located between New York and Boston.”

Buyers should note that “the antique barn is being sold in as-is condition,” according to the listing.

#5645. Kyndryl shares surge 30% on hyperscaler-related revenue growth

Shares of Kyndryl Holdings Inc. jumped 30% today after it reported better-than-expected earnings for the second quarter of its 2027 fiscal year.

Kyndryl generated $3.9 billion in sales during the three months ended Sept. 30. That represents a 1.9% decrease from a year earlier, but the company still managed to top the consensus estimate by about $50 million. It attributed the top-line surprise to its Kyndryl Consult business.

Kyndryl, a former IBM Corp. unit, once generated nearly all its revenue from managing other companies’ technology infrastructure. In 2022, it launched Kyndryl Consult to take on more strategic, higher-margin professional services deals.

The unit’s revenue grew 4.2% year-over-year in the second quarter. Kyndryl didn’t share a specific quarterly revenue number, but divulged that the unit earned a total of $3.6 billion over the past 12 months.

Kyndryl Consult’s signings, a measure of future revenue, jumped 19% over the past year. That momentum may have contributed to the company’s stock rally today.

Many of the projects that Kyndryl Consult takes on involve artificial intelligence. The unit can help customers build AI agent ensembles and set up training data generation pipelines. Additionally, it can advise clients about business decisions such as how they should allocate their AI budgets.

Kyndryl offers a software platform called Bridge to companies that buy its AI services. It enables AI agents to access business data from an organization’s internal systems. Additionally, Bridge monitors those agents to ensure they adhere to safety requirements.

The public cloud is another major focus of Kyndryl’s growth efforts. The company’s hyperscale-related revenue topped $500 million in the second quarter, which amounts to a 27% year-over-year increase.

“Strong signings and continued growth in Kyndryl Consult and hyperscaler-related revenue reinforce our confidence in our fiscal 2027 outlook,” said Kyndryl Chief Executive Officer Martin Schroeter. “Our performance reflects demand for Kyndryl’s AI-led modernization capabilities and deep mission-critical expertise that help customers evolve their complex technology environments, strengthen cybersecurity and achieve measurable business outcomes.”

The company delivered an adjusted net income of $92 million, which breaks down to 42 cents per share. Analysts expected 41 cents per share. The sum excludes a $38 million workforce reduction charge the company took in the second quarter. It’s part of a broader cost-cutting initiative that is set to save up to $500 million annually starting from Kyndryl’s 2028 fiscal year.

For the current fiscal year, the company is forecasting an adjusted pretax income of $600 million to $700 million. Kyndryl expects its revenue to be flat or increase by up to 2%.

#5644. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5643. Phaze raises $8.75M to give AI agents remote access to powerful workstations

If autonomous artificial intelligence agents are really going to become the future of the enterprise then they’re going to need to have a computer of their own so they can get on with their work without disturbing anyone else.

The founders of the remote desktop firm Parsec Technologies Inc. have come up with a new offering that’s designed to give those agents the computer access they need. Their new startup is called Phaze Inc., and it has just launched its offering after raising $8.75 million in seed funding from Andreessen Horowitz. Today’s round also saw participation from Index, NextView, Makers and Lerer Hippeau.

Phaze has developed a high-performance remote desktop platform that’s designed to accommodate both humans and AI agent workers, giving them access to powerful computers, including high-end workstations. With its platform, those users can control a distant workstation with the same low-latency responsiveness and visual fidelity they’d get if they were accessing hardware locally.

The startup says it’s trying to solve a couple of glaring efficiency problems at many enterprises. One issue is the emergence of computer-use agents that like to hijack worker’s screens while automating mundane business tasks, reducing human productivity.

Another challenge is that many enterprises invest in powerful workstations capable of rendering complex 3D graphics and compiling massive codebases that can cost upwards of $10,000. Those machines are needed, but many information technology departments tend to have a policy of assigning one machine to each employee, which means that expensive hardware is often left sitting idle if that person goes out for lunch, sits in a meeting or takes a few days off.

Phaze’s solution is to transform those workstations into a shared pool of elastic compute, allowing anyone at an organization to access it via its proprietary low-latency streaming technology when they need it. This streaming tech is backed by a specially developed Model Context Protocol server that allows computer use agents to log into and operate expensive workstations the same way a human employee would.

The result: Instead of working exclusively through expensive and brittle application programming interfaces, agents can access a computer directly and navigate its operating system, launch applications and get work done.

Phaze co-founder and Chief Executive Benjy Boxer said the platform also supports human-to-agent collaboration, so they can work together to get more complex tasks done. For instance, an automated IT support bot might work to diagnose problems when new tickets are created, and then pass the session to a human engineer if the solution is more nuanced than what it’s authorized to do by itself.

“The computer sitting on your desk shouldn’t determine what compute you can access,” Boxer said. “People need powerful workstations to do their jobs, and now AI agents need computers they can actually operate. We’re building the access layer that lets either one connect to the machine they need, wherever it happens to be.”

By transforming expensive workstations into shared infrastructure, administrators can assign their computing resources dynamically to whoever needs access as people’s and agent’s workflows fluctuate. The workstations themselves can be sat on a desk, installed in a data center, or locked away in a cupboard. Wherever they’re located, organizations will be able to get maximum efficiency out of them.

Phaze’s job now is to convince enterprises of the benefits of its platform, and Boxer said the money from today’s round will be used to accelerate its go-to-market plans and onboard new customers. The startup will also look to expand its engineering team and develop more features.

Andreessen Horowitz General Partner Martin Casado think Phaze is likely to see a lot of interest in its remote access platform, because workstations are too expensive to be left sitting idle for hours at a time. “Phaze is turning those machines into shared infrastructure for people and AI agents,” he said. “Benjy and the team have been building in this space for more than a decade and they bring that experience to a new era of remote access and machine management.”

#5642. ‘It’s H for Housing’: How Texas Democrats Plan To Build on GOP Homebuilding Momentum

Texas enacted some of its most consequential housing supply reforms in years under Republican leadership, but Tuesday's historic Democratic sweep in the Lone Star State has suddenly opened the door to changes advocates thought were politically impossible.

“The boundaries shifted entirely for the possibilities for low-income households and Texans seeking affordability,” Texas Housers, a nonprofit housing advocacy organization, tells Realtor.com®. "What was realistic 24 hours ago is dramatically different from what is realistic today.”

Among those possibilities are greater state investment in affordable housing, stronger renter protections, and more funding to rebuild homes damaged by natural disasters—priorities the organization hopes the incoming administration will advance.

But the state's homebuilding industry is looking to build on an agenda it has spent years advancing with officials from both parties.

"It's neither D nor R. It's H for housing," Scott Norman, CEO of the Texas Association of Builders, tells Realtor.com.

After an election shaped by pocketbook concerns, Texas' new guard will doubtless be judged on whether it can solve for Norman's 'H'—turning the momentum of the nation's most active homebuilding market into homes more Texans can afford.

Texas' Republican-led Legislature had already begun dismantling barriers to housing construction before Tuesday's election.

Senate Bill 840, for example, allows developers to convert certain commercial properties into apartments without extensive rezoning.

Since taking effect in September 2025, the law has enabled plans for at least 8,400 apartments, according to a July analysis by the Texas Tribune citing a coalition of housing reform advocates. That's equivalent to roughly one-fifth of the multifamily units permitted statewide during the period.

That’s an especially notable share given that the Lone Star State leads the nation in homebuilding, issuing more permits than any other state and accounting for 14.6% of building permits issued nationwide, according to the latest Affordability and Homebuilding Report Cards from Realtor.com.

But to Norman's point, it was a bipartisan push—one that Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa helped advance during her time in the state Legislature. As a member of the House Land & Resource Management Committee, she voted in favor of moving SB 840 forward.

It's something Norman hasn’t forgotten, saying she was "supportive of stuff we were pushing" during the previous legislative session. "I'm sure and I know she'll take that experience to the governor's mansion.”

Tray Bates, vice president of governmental affairs at Texas Realtors, also sees room for cooperation.

"The core problem is supply," Bates tells Realtor.com. "Texas is adding people faster than it's adding homes people can afford."

Both organizations want to continue easing restrictions on residential development, while Norman also sees an opportunity to address the shortage of skilled construction workers through expanded workforce training.

"The more folks we can get in the business, that'll drive down those labor costs," he says.

But Texas' homebuilding boom has done far less to close the gap for its lowest-income renters.

The state faces a shortage of 709,000 affordable and available rentals for extremely low-income households, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition.

Texas Housers argues that insufficient state investment has contributed to that shortfall.

"Texas has relied almost entirely on federal dollars and tax credits to create and preserve affordable housing in our communities," the organization says. "Current resources are not enough to address the need for safe, decent, and affordable housing."

Indeed, just $10.1 million in state funding was allocated to the Housing Trust Fund for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. By contrast, the state awarded more than $114 million in federal housing tax credits to help finance affordable rental units in 2026 alone.

The programs serve different purposes, to be sure, but the figures illustrate how heavily Texas relies on federal incentives to finance affordable rental development.

Land Commissioner-elect Ben Flores sees another opportunity in the approximately 13 million acres managed by the General Land Office.

"We [sic] hold parcels near growing cities that are sitting idle," Flores tells Realtor.com. "My team will inventory those parcels and identify which ones could support housing for teachers, nurses, first responders, and working families through long-term leases that keep the land in public hands and still earn revenue for the Permanent School Fund.

"Housing and school funding don't have to compete," he adds. "Done right, they support each other."

Flores intends to prioritize the Houston region and Rio Grande Valley, where he says rising housing costs have compounded the challenges facing families recovering from floods.

He's also promising to address delays in distributing disaster recovery aid—an issue Texas Housers says has left some Hurricane Harvey survivors waiting years to rebuild.

"When the state relies solely on federal dollars run through slow, unaccountable systems, the families with the least end up waiting the longest," the organization says.

Flores says he'll tackle this head-on in his first 90 days by conducting an agency audit, with public progress reports every 30 days and measurable targets for distributing assistance.

"We will review every open recovery program, find out where funds are stuck and why, and work to get those dollars back to hurricane survivors," Flores says. "Allocation decisions will be made based on need and damage, not politics, and we'll publish where the money is going so Texans can see it for themselves."

Renters could also see a different approach under the incoming administration.

"Basic tenant protections are also urgently needed," Texas Housers says, calling for eviction record sealing and greater transparency around rental fees among its legislative priorities.

Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin has proposed property tax incentives for landlords who maintain affordable rents, while Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has promised a 30-day review of consumer protection and competition laws, specifically identifying algorithmic rent-setting as an enforcement concern.

Then there are the forces outside what any single public office can control—forces that Norman argues will be the greater determinants of Texas' housing future.

"Two things that drive housing growth are population growth and job growth," he says.

And there’s been no shortage of that in Texas. The state has added more than 2.6 million residents since 2020, according to U.S. Census Bureau figures.

When asked about fears that growth could stall or reverse, Norman responds with enthusiastic optimism that the state's economic appeal will continue attracting households and supporting construction.

But some real estate professionals outside the state are watching for signs that the political shift could change where affluent residents choose to live.

Miltiadis Kastanis, a Miami Beach luxury real estate agent with Compass, says inquiries from Texas buyers were rising before the election.

"We have noticed an increase in inquiries from the Texan market," he says.

Kastanis believes the latest political shifts could accelerate that interest, particularly among wealthy Texans concerned about future changes to the state's tax environment.

"You will see Texans start pre-planning a move to the Florida market," he says, but he cautions against expecting a mass exodus or COVID-19 pandemic-era bidding wars.

Bates is similarly skeptical that one election will significantly alter migration patterns.

"It's far too early to predict migration based on one election," he says. "Domestic migration to Texas was already slowing before Tuesday, and housing costs are a major factor."

And at a crossroads for Texas housing policy, that could become a North Star for housing advocates, industry leaders, and the incoming administration alike.

"Maybe the policy solutions may look a little different based on who's in charge," Norman says, but the commitment to a more affordable Texas remains the same.

"There's a lot we can get done with the new folks coming in," he says.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5641. Econ Review: A Look at October’s Key Market Data

Editor’s note: Econ Review is a roundup of the housing and economic market data reports released during the month.

As the winter slowdown draws closer, the housing market remains in a sticky spot as the economy continues to face challenges trickling down from the Iran War. Now moving toward the end of 2026, the question remains whether we’ll begin to see a housing market recovery next year.

Let’s take a look at what the housing and economic data reports released in October can show us:

Existing-home sales saw a slight boost as the summer season finally came to a close, up 1.5% month-over-month in the latest report. Some regions picked up as well, with the South and West recording month-over-month gains.

Despite a slight monthly uptick, National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun noted in the report that the end of summer—August and September—marked “the two slowest months for home sales this year.”

As such, existing-home sales remained depleted year-over-year by 2.2%. All four regions also saw losses year-over-year.

Ali Wolf, chief economist at NewHomeSource and Zonda, said that the uptick was not an indicator of marker recovery as “supply is still pulling most of the weight here.”

“Today’s report shows a market clearing accumulated listings, not a wave of buyers coming in,” she continued. “And, this is the last clean read before mortgage rates shot up to over 7%, meaning next month we’ll start to see the impact on buyer activity.”

A positive note in the report was a slightly increased share of first-time buyers, as Realtor.com® Chief Economist Danielle Hale said that the market is “past the worst of the starter-home supply crunch nationwide, which may help entry-level buyers gain a foothold.”

In addition, existing-home inventory remains on the rise, growing 1.9% month-over-month and 4.6% year-over-year.

Construction challenges kept new-home sales muted for another month, falling 0.6% month-over-month and 5.3% year-over-year. Additionally, last month’s sales numbers were also revised downward by about 0.6%, dimming activity further.

“Builders continue to offer incentives and adjust pricing to attract buyers, but elevated mortgage rates and high home prices are limiting the number of households that can afford to purchase a home,” said National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) Chairman Bill Owens.

Wolf also predicted a potential increase in new-home sales in the fall and winter due to the incentives being offered by builders to “meet their year-end goals,” making it the “prime season for new home shopping.”

Looking ahead at potential activity, mortgage rates back up in the 7% range are starting to weigh on the market as pending home sales dropped 7.3% month-over-month and 11.3% year-over-year. All four regions also experienced declines on both a monthly and annual basis.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones noted that elevated rates are definitely “deteriorating” the market, and “this month’s deep freeze in buyer activity could persist until affordability improves.”

“The local data confirms that higher rates are impacting buyers throughout the country, even in markets that have shown consistent strength,” she continued.

However, Jones added that even though rates are straining buyer budgets, “the market is becoming more hospitable for those who can afford to participate.”

“Lower prices, a slower pace and more price reductions may help offset some of the impact of higher rates,” she concluded.

The latest Case-Shiller Index saw real home values decline for the 15th straight month as inflation continues to outpace home-price growth.

Home-price growth did see a slight uplift this month, advancing from 1.9% year-over-over growth last month to 2.1% in the latest report. The 10- and 20-City Composites were also both up 0.2% in their annual gains to 3.6% and 2.7%, respectively.

Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of Commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices, did note a discrepancy in seasonally adjusted and non-seasonally adjusted prices (declines vs. rises, respectively), which she explained is indicative of a “post-summer slowdown” that “is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices.”

Kaufman also cautioned that affordability will still face challenges as inflation rises due to gas, oil and energy prices rising.

“Households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices,” she said.

As for existing homes, the median existing-home price clocked in at $417,500, which is a 1.3% annual increase. This is a reversal from last month’s 1.2% annual fall, but still a lower rate of growth than historical peaks.

As previously mentioned, housing construction’s challenges have kept the industry segment fairly muted throughout the year, and this month was no expectation.

The latest New Residential Construction report saw housing starts drop 5.2% month-over-month and 7.4% year-over-year, led by 7.2% month-over-month and a whopping 25.9% year-over-year fall in multifamily starts (which had previously been performing well). Single-family starts also remained diminished with a 4.6% fall month-over-month, but did see a slight year-over-year improvement of +2.6%.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington—NAHB’s assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis—noted that this month’s data “align(s) with our forecast of lower production in 2026, with further declines expected in 2027 as rates stay elevated and material costs rise.”

Despite starts remaining diminished, housing completions did see a slight month-over-month uptick by 2.2%. The slight monthly boost is likely due to a 14.9% month-over-month boost in multifamily completions. However, overall completions were still well down year-over-year by 14%, as single-family completions were down across the board and multifamily completions were down year-over-year.

In addition, the fall in multifamily starts may not last for long, as multifamily permits were up 5.9% month-over-month and 1% year-over-year. Overall, permits had the smallest fall in the report, down only 0.2% month-over-month and 3% year-over-year.

“The market is not conducive to building right now, and the diminished starts and completions figures make that clear,” added Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner. “However, the relative resiliency of new home permitting shows that builders see these conditions as temporary.”

With construction reports still coming in well below historical norms, builder confidence remains fairly shaken. The latest Housing Market Index actually saw builder confidence tank to a 14-year low, clocking in at 29 (out of 100, with 50 being the baseline).

The “Trump administration’s efforts to advance regulatory reform” are, according to NAHB Chairman Owens, “helping to ease some of the cost pressures (builders) face.” Nevertheless, the administration’s immigration crackdown is “causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work.”

Price cuts and incentives are still being heavily used by builders to sell new homes, with the share of builders enacting price cuts actually peaking to a six-year high at 43%.

The labor market has seen a lot of resilience in recent months, but this month’s jobs report unfortunately weakened and lost some ground.

The unemployment rate—which has been unchanged at 4.1% for the past two months—saw a slight uptick to 4.2%. Only 29,000 jobs were added this month, which is below economists’ expectations in the range of 80,000.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel called the report a “clear miss,” but noted that it probably wouldn’t change that much when it came time for the Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.

“Despite tepid September job growth, unemployment remains low, so in short, this is no labor disaster that would pull the FOMC’s focus off inflation,” he continued.

Krimmel also pointed toward the downward revisions in added jobs over the past two months, explaining that the unemployment rate’s increase is not as severe as people may believe.

“Layoffs haven’t picked up, and jobless claims have been falling, so the low-hire, low-fire market is likely to stay entrenched as we head into 2027,” he said.

Speaking of inflation, the latest Consumer Price Index saw an increase as inflation remains elevated, now clocking in at 3.7% and core inflation at 2.6%. Krimmel noted that these figures “came in slightly hotter than expected,” and potentially point to a Fed rate hike by December.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index also recorded an increase this month, hitting 3.6% annual inflation and 3.1% core annual inflation. Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long said that “inflation is back near a 3-year high,” which is “largely due to war in Iran.”

Long also identified other major reasons for inflation—a “(b)ig rise in goods prices,” “service sector inflation” and “sideways” housing inflation as indicative of rising core inflation in general.

The Fed ended up not making any changes to rates, despite many predictions leaning in that direction. However, further rate hikes remain on the table.

Notably, Realtor.com Chief Economist Hale anticipated another two to three hikes over the next six to eight months, which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5% to 4.75%.

Consumer opinions were slightly mixed this month, as sentiment remained flat while confidence saw an increase.

Sentiment’s lack of movement was largely attributed to the prolonged conflict with Iran. Also, despite little movement this month, sentiment has honed in on a 74-year low in the survey’s history.

Confidence, on the other hand, grew due to growth in positive perceptions of current and expected business conditions. This was attributed to the brief recovery seen in gas prices from September to October. Confidence does, however, remain on the downward trend it has been on over recent years, the report noted.

Looking ahead, the Leading Economic Index registered flat this month as the economy remains challenged due to the aforementioned elevation in inflation. The report was also not indicative of any recession in the coming months.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5640. Ocient raises $100 million as agentic AI drives growth in large-scale analytics

Ocient Inc., the maker of a speedy data analytics platform, today said it has raised $100 million in a Series C funding to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business.

That business is fueled by growing demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers seeking to analyze massive datasets without sampling. The new round brings the Chicago-based company’s total funding to $260 million.

Ocient said it expects revenue to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling revenue the previous year. The company said the new financing will accelerate delivery of its OcientAIQ Solutions, which enable AI agents and human analysts to query petabyte-scale datasets.

Chief Executive John Morris said much of the growth is coming from new customers in national security and telecommunications, particularly organizations using the platform to consolidate cybersecurity information.

“They’ve been accustomed to having to sample data coming off the network,” Morris said. “They don’t have anything that can handle the ingest rates, nor that can store at an affordable price tens of petabytes of data.”

Ocient’s original business focused on high-performance analytics, but the emergence of AI agents has expanded its potential market. Increasingly, software agents rather than human analysts are querying its systems, driving higher utilization and creating demand for more comprehensive datasets.

The OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration. Its architecture minimizes data movement and uses forward error correction instead of conventional replication to provide data protection with reduced storage overhead.

“The architecture is designed not to move data around constantly as most architectures do, and to have nothing replicated,” Morris said.

The company competes with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and open-source analytics implementations, although its technology frequently complements existing platforms rather than replacing them, the CEO said.

Cybersecurity has emerged as a particularly promising market. Ocient provides the underlying data infrastructure that enables security tools and AI agents to analyze network activity across complete historical datasets, potentially identifying threats that conventional sampling would miss.

However, Morris said the company isn’t positioned as a cybersecurity tool. “We don’t do the detection algorithms and the sort of things that the companies in that space do,” Morris said.

Government and defense customers account for a substantial portion of Ocient’s business. The company recently established a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve those markets.

Morris said the new funding should be sufficient to help Ocient reach breakeven, although he declined to provide a timetable. Ocient plans to direct much of the investment toward hiring sales and customer delivery personnel while continuing engineering development.

The company is also seeing increasing demand for on-premises deployments as customers seek greater control over costs and sensitive information. “Most of our opportunities now are on-prem because they’re either repatriating for cost reasons or for data sovereignty and data protection issues,” Morris said.

The company is also looking to expand geographically, particularly in Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, while pursuing additional cybersecurity customers.

The round was co-led by Boka Capital Ltd. and OCA Ventures LLC, with participation from previous investors Greycroft Partners LLC, In-Q-Tel Inc., Blue Bear Capital LLC, Buoyant Ventures Management LLC, PSP Partners LLC’s PSP Growth fund and Pritzker Group Venture Capital LLC.
